**Summary.** This work analyzes the phase diagram of the transverse-field ANNNI model, demonstrating how quantum fluctuations drive the system through a sequence of ordered magnetic phases analogous to the Fisher-Selke sequence. By combining high-order perturbation theory with advanced quantum Monte Carlo simulations, the authors confirm the stability and relative ordering of these phases, particularly noting the unique suppression effect observed in the bilayer extension.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between quantum fluctuations and the emergence of sequences mirroring classical critical phenomena (Fisher-Selke sequence) in an extended magnetic model is highly relevant for understanding quantum phase transitions in lattice systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the onset and stability of various ordered magnetic structures within the transverse-field Axial Next-Nearest-Neighbor Ising (ANNNI) model, both on a single layer and in a bilayer.

**Main result.** Quantum fluctuations select a sequence of ordered phases ($\langle 3 angle$, $\langle 23 angle$, etc.) whose emergence follows the pattern of the classical Fisher-Selke sequence, with the bilayer structure suppressing these successive phases.

**Method.** The research combines high-order perturbation theory in the transverse field ($g$) with Stochastic Series Expansion (SSE) quantum Monte Carlo simulations to calculate free energies and compare competing ordered states.

**Model / system.** The system is the transverse-field ANNNI model defined on a square lattice, extended to a bilayer. The Hamiltonian includes nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor Ising interactions, along with a transverse field term ($\Gamma \sum \sigma^x$).

**Key observables.** Energy per spin ($e$), transverse magnetization ($m_x$), and the free energies of competing ordered states ($\langle 3 angle$, $\langle 2 angle$, $\langle 23 angle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The critical parameters include the ratio of next-nearest-neighbor to nearest-neighbor coupling ($\kappa = J_2/J_0$) and the transverse field strength ($g = \Gamma/J_0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on perturbation theory up to $g^8$ and rigorous comparison of simulation results across multiple lattice sizes and simulation protocols to establish phase stability.

**Figures summary.** The notes refer to figures illustrating the low-field phase diagram near the multiphase point, showing crossings and the stability windows for different ordered phases.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the classical ground state degeneracy at $\kappa=1/2$. It then uses perturbation theory to determine the leading quantum corrections, identifying the sequence of phases ($\langle 3 angle 	o \langle 23 angle 	o \dots$). Finally, it uses quantum Monte Carlo simulations to confirm these theoretical predictions, especially in the bilayer geometry.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the transverse-field axial next-nearest-neighbor Ising (ANNNI) model on the square lattice and on a bilayer. At the classical multiphase point $κ=J_2/J_0=1/2$, every configuration of straight domain walls that separates domains of at least two sites is a ground state. The walls are rigid, so perturbation theory in the transverse field $g=Γ/J_0$ can be carried out for each configuration separately, and we take it to order $g^8$. Quantum fluctuations select $\langle 3\rangle$ ($\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\downarrow\downarrow$) at order $g^2$, because spins next to a wall gain the most energy from virtual flips. The structures $\langle 23\rangle$, $\langle 223\rangle$ and $\langle 2223\rangle$ then open between $\langle 3\rangle$ and the antiphase $\langle 2\rangle$ at orders $g^4$, $g^6$ and $g^8$, in the order of the Fisher-Selke sequence of the classical three-dimensional model. A second layer suppresses each successive phase more strongly, beyond the stiffening of the local fields. We test the two widest phases with stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo, comparing the free energies of the competing ordered states by thermodynamic integration, since annealing freezes in the modulation that forms at the ordering transition. The simulations reproduce the $\langle 3\rangle$ wedge to about 1%, and in a pre-registered test $\langle 23\rangle$ is stable at six of seven points, with the seventh resolved by post-hoc runs.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a rigorous quantum cavity method to develop polynomial-time classical and quantum algorithms for mean-field models. It successfully estimates thermal expectations for both classical spin glasses (Ising model) and quantum systems (SYK model) up to their respective phase transitions. This work provides significant algorithmic advances for analyzing strongly correlated and disordered quantum matter.

**Why it may be interesting.** The development of the quantum cavity method provides a powerful, rigorous tool for analyzing complex, highly interacting quantum systems like SYK, bridging the gap between mean-field theory and exact results in a way that is applicable to quantum information and many-body physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is developing polynomial-time classical and quantum algorithms to estimate local thermal expectations for mean-field models, especially in regimes approaching a glass transition.

**Main result.** The authors prove polynomial-time classical algorithms for estimating thermal expectations in the Ising p-spin model up to its glass transition, and for the SYK model at any constant temperature. They also provide a quantum algorithm to learn the SYK Hamiltonian from the Gibbs state.

**Method.** The primary technique is the development and application of a rigorous quantum cavity method, which allows for the control of expectations and concentration around the saddle point in the thermodynamic limit.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on mean-field models, specifically the classical Ising p-spin model (exhibiting spin glass behavior) and the quantum Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, both characterized by dense random interactions.

**Key observables.** Local thermal expectations of operators (e.g., spin expectations for Ising, $	ext{Tr}(\mathcal{O} e^{-eta H}) / 	ext{Tr}(e^{-eta H})$ for SYK).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Inverse temperature ($eta$), system size ($N$), and the critical temperature/transition point ($eta^*$ or any constant $eta > 0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The classical algorithms rely on the assumption that typical instances concentrate around the saddle point, and the quantum cavity method requires establishing factorization properties to control errors.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the classical prediction of thermal observables for the SYK model, comparing results across different system sizes and increasing Hermite degree, showing convergence to the infinite-$N$ prediction.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the quantum cavity method to rigorously control expectations in mean-field models. It applies this method first to the classical Ising model to solve the open question of computing expectations up to the glass transition, and then to the quantum SYK model for calculating thermal expectations and learning its Hamiltonian.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model is a strongly interacting fermionic system that has been well-studied in condensed matter and high energy physics. It is highly quantum: Gaussian states are far from the thermal state (Hastings and O'Donnell, STOC'22) and representing the thermal state requires large polynomial-size quantum circuits (Anschuetz et al., QIP'25). Very recently, it was nonetheless proven that classical algorithms can estimate local thermal expectations at sufficiently high temperature in quasipolynomial time (Zlokapa, FOCS'26). We show that classical algorithms can in fact estimate local observables at all constant temperatures in polynomial time. Our techniques also extend straightforwardly to classical systems: we resolve an open question about computing thermal expectations of a classical spin glass up to its phase transition (Bencs et al., STOC'26). Our proof develops a fully rigorous quantum cavity method. Due to the success of the classical cavity method in optimization, sampling, inference and learning, we expect the quantum cavity method to find further applications of independent interest. As an example, we give a quantum algorithm that learns SYK Hamiltonians from the Gibbs state at any constant temperature with polynomial time and sample complexity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents an efficient, dimension-free algorithm for shadow tomography, estimating many expectation values of an unknown quantum state. It achieves a complexity scaling of $O(\log(m) \log(m/\delta)/\epsilon^2)$ copies. The method cleverly uses the average-case setting combined with the minimax theorem to establish a strong worst-case guarantee.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides state-of-the-art complexity bounds for quantum state characterization, which is fundamental for quantum characterization protocols in quantum computing and quantum sensing.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses shadow tomography: estimating the expectation values of a large set of observables $\{O_1, \dots, O_m\}$ for an unknown quantum state $ho$ using multiple copies of $ho$.

**Main result.** They derive an algorithm requiring $O(\log(m) \log(m/\delta)/\epsilon^2)$ copies to estimate all expectation values within $\pm\epsilon$ with high probability.

**Method.** The approach leverages the average-case setting, utilizing Pretty Good Measurements (PGM) and applying Sion's minimax theorem to lift the average-case guarantee to a worst-case guarantee.

**Model / system.** The system involves an unknown quantum state $ho$ and a set of $m$ observables $\{O_i\}$. The analysis is general, focusing on the complexity scaling with the number of observables $m$.

**Key observables.** The expectation values $	ext{tr}(O_iho)$ for $i \in [m]$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The complexity scales with $m$ (number of observables), $\epsilon$ (accuracy), and $\delta$ (failure probability).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on the average-case formulation and the non-constructive implication from the minimax theorem. A key limitation is the remaining $\log(m)$ factor separating the quantum problem from its classical one.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the algorithm by first establishing bounds in the average-case setting, then using the minimax principle to claim the worst-case bound. It concludes by identifying inherent limitations in the approach.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We give a shadow tomography algorithm that uses $O(\log(m) \log(m/δ) / \varepsilon^2)$ copies of the input state. Specifically, given a quantum state $ρ$ and observables $O_1,\ldots,O_m$, the algorithm outputs estimates of $\mathrm{tr}(O_iρ)$ for all $i\in[m]$ that are all accurate to within $\pm\varepsilon$, except with probability at most $δ$. The key idea is to work in the average-case setting: for a random state drawn from a known prior, a pretty good measurement on $O(\log(m)/\varepsilon^2)$ copies gives a constant-error guarantee on all but a small fraction of the prior. Boosting this guarantee gives an average-case shadow tomography algorithm, and the minimax principle then (non-constructively) implies the existence of a measurement with the same worst-case guarantee.   We also identify an obstruction to further improvement with this approach. While pretty good measurements amplify success over the randomness of the prior, they do not amplify success over the randomness of measurement. This issue appears to be inherent, and gives rise to the remaining $\log(m)$ factor separating the complexity of the quantum problem from its classical counterpart.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a precise mathematical framework to bridge the gap between continuous unitary quantum evolution and its discrete approximation via products of unitaries. It proves that time-stepping and Hamiltonian truncation methods yield approximations with controlled error bounds, thereby allowing continuous adiabatic theorems to be directly translated to finite-precision quantum circuits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides the necessary theoretical machinery to rigorously connect continuous physical models (like those studied in AMO or quantum optics) to the discrete gate-based implementations required by quantum computers, quantifying the associated errors.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of relating continuous unitary quantum evolution, governed by a time-dependent Hamiltonian, to its practical approximation using finite products of unitaries achievable in digital quantum computation.

**Main result.** It establishes a rigorous, bidirectional correspondence between continuous unitary evolutions and products of unitaries, providing explicit error bounds of $O(1/T)$ for the time-discretization process.

**Method.** The approach involves comparing continuous evolution (using methods like Duhamel estimates) with discrete approximations derived from time-step sampling or Hamiltonian truncation, while also extending these bounds to adiabatic processes.

**Model / system.** The model is general unitary evolution $U(T)$ generated by a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(t)$. The analysis applies to quantum linear systems and general Hamiltonians requiring bounded derivatives and spectral gaps.

**Key observables.** Operator-norm distance error bounds ($O(1/T)$), leakage bounds (related to the Davis–Kahan theorem), and the comparison between continuous and discrete adiabatic bounds.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Total time $T$, number of steps $T$, spectral gap $\Gamma$, condition number $\kappa$, and error $\delta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes bounded first and second derivatives of $H(t)$, bounded spectral width, and eigenvalue differences bounded away from zero multiples of $2\pi$.

**Paper structure.** The paper is structured by first defining continuous evolutions, then developing techniques for bit truncation and fine-step comparison, followed by comparing truncation levels and time sampling, and finally applying these results to adiabatic theorems and quantum linear systems.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

I present a short approach to discretizing continuous unitary evolution. It gives a correspondence in both directions between continuous unitary evolutions and products of unitaries in finite dimensions, and I use it to reduce discrete adiabatic theorems to continuous ones. At fine steps, holding truncated samples of a regulated Hamiltonian on a suitable finite partition gives an approximating product. Conversely, rounding the clock identifies a product of $T$ unit-step samples with a continuous evolution, up to two half-step phases. I bound its operator-norm distance from the original evolution by $O(1/T)$ through cancellation within each time step. This assumes bounded first and second derivatives, bounded spectral width, and eigenvalue differences bounded away from nonzero multiples of $2π$, uniformly in $T$. For a unitary walk with these derivative bounds, a fixed common free spectral arc supplies a Hermitian logarithm path satisfying the comparison hypotheses. Continuous simulation guarantees then transfer to the phase-corrected product, and continuous adiabatic bounds to the product itself, with an explicit additive $O(1/T)$ error and each adiabatic theorem's hypotheses retained. For positive definite quantum linear systems of condition number $κ$, this comparison and continuous adiabatic theory give a rescaled qubitized walk with $O(κ/δ)$ steps for leakage $δ$, matching the scaling previously obtained through a discrete adiabatic theorem. These products need no discrete adiabatic theorem.

</details>

**Summary.** This work rigorously analyzes the quantum leakage in Shamir secret sharing schemes when devices utilize correlated quantum resources. By employing advanced techniques like Fourier analysis and marginal comparison, the authors establish that the leakage is exponentially small under certain conditions. This provides strong theoretical guarantees for the security of quantum information protocols.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous, quantitative security bounds for quantum secret sharing protocols, which is fundamental to quantum cryptography and secure quantum computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper quantifies the quantum leakage that occurs during Shamir secret sharing when the quantum resources used by the sharing devices are correlated.

**Main result.** It proves that the leakage state exhibits an exponentially small trace distance between any two secrets, provided the reconstruction requires a sufficiently large fraction of the shares.

**Method.** The analysis uses advanced tools from quantum information theory, including Fourier analysis, bounding marginals by product states, and establishing exponential decay rates based on the required share fraction.

**Model / system.** The model is Shamir's secret sharing scheme applied to quantum resources ($\Omega$), where devices operate on their classical shares to emit qubits. The analysis considers fixed stationary quantum chains and primitive quantum memories.

**Key observables.** Trace distance ($	ext{Adv}(ho, \sigma)$) between leakage states, and the optimal exponential base for leakage decay.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The fraction of shares required for reconstruction ($t/n$), the dimension of the output qubits ($d$), and the structure of the quantum memory (primitive transfer channels).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results assume the quantum resources are generated by fixed stationary chains satisfying an upper operator mixing condition and primitive quantum memories.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from analyzing independent device-reference pairs using Fourier bounds, extends this to correlated resources via marginal comparison, and finally establishes general exponential security guarantees for various resource models.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study leakage from Shamir secret sharing when each device uses its share to produce one qubit from an initial quantum resource independent of the secret and sharing randomness. We prove exponentially small trace distance between the leakage states of any two secrets, when reconstruction requires a sufficiently large fraction of the shares, for fixed stationary chains satisfying an upper operator mixing condition and for resources generated by fixed finite quantum memories with primitive transfer channels. These guarantees permit arbitrary extensions of the device marginal as adversary side information and hold uniformly over prime fields larger than the number of shares. For independent device--reference pairs, which provide the quantitative input to the argument, we determine the optimal exponential base when reconstruction requires all shares: $2\sqrt2/π$ for a qubit and $2/π$ for a classical bit, in both cases allowing arbitrary finite references. A comparison of selected marginals with product states converts the bounds for independent device--reference pairs into security guarantees for the correlated resources.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the critical issue of frequency crowding in superconducting quantum processors, which limits scalability through crosstalk. It formulates the problem as a Max-k-Cut optimization, developing a Hamiltonian framework that incorporates multiple collision mechanisms. The resulting methodology enables systematic, hardware-aware frequency planning, connecting microscopic physics to large-scale processor design.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the physical constraints limiting qubit connectivity and scaling in superconducting quantum hardware by providing a systematic, physics-informed optimization tool.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Frequency crowding, caused by close spacing of qubit transitions, severely limits the scalability of superconducting quantum processors due to crosstalk and leakage errors.

**Main result.** The authors developed a hardware-aware optimization framework that maps collision penalties to a Max-k-Cut problem, showing that counterdiabatic QAOA and simulated annealing can systematically solve for optimal, collision-free qubit frequency assignments.

**Method.** The problem is formulated using a Hamiltonian-based framework, mapping collision mechanisms (two- and three-body) onto a discrete cost function solved via quantum optimization algorithms (QAOA) and classical solvers (Simulated Annealing).

**Model / system.** The system is superconducting quantum processors using transmon qubits, modeled by a cost Hamiltonian $H_C$ that includes penalties for nearest-neighbor collisions ($A_1$), gate clashes ($C_1$), and spectator effects ($S_1$).

**Key observables.** Collision penalties (cost function), gate and idle fidelities, and the resulting frequency-collision landscape.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Frequency spacing ($\Delta = 0.5 	ext{ GHz}$), operating frequency ($\omega = 5.5 	ext{ GHz}$), and the specific collision types (A1, C1, S1).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The leading collision terms ($A_1, C_1, S_1$) dominate the landscape, allowing higher-order terms to be neglected in the initial modeling.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the framework flow from initial assignment to the final collision-free map. Figure 2 shows the hardware penalty function landscape for two coupled qubits, defining safe operating valleys.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the physical problem, formulates it as a Max-k-Cut problem using a detailed collision Hamiltonian, develops scalable protocols like cluster-stitching, and benchmarks various optimization algorithms (DC-QAOA, QAOA, SA).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Frequency crowding, the close spacing of qubit transitions, limits superconducting quantum processors through crosstalk, leakage, and spectator dependent errors. We introduce a Hamiltonian based framework that maps two- and three-body collision mechanisms onto a Max-k-Cut problem on qubit frequency allocation. In order to make larger lattices tractable, we introduce a cluster-stitching protocol that decomposes larger lattices into overlapping subgraphs and reconciles their local frequency assignments into globally consistent configurations. We tested our proposed framework across multiple qubit architectures to suppress dominant collision penalties by revealing a hardware residual crosstalk. We benchmark digitized counterdiabatic QAOA (DC-QAOA), standard QAOA, and simulated annealing. Counterdiabatic terms improve QAOA optimization near steep collision penalties, while simulated annealing achieves the lowest costs on the tested instances. These results indicate that our hardware-aware optimization connects microscopic interaction physics to processor-level frequency planning. These results enable a systematic solver for benchmarking of scalable software hardware co design.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a theoretical method to test if a quantum state is Gaussian (bosonic or fermionic) using only a constant number of copies, a significant improvement over previous scaling results. The proof leverages advanced techniques involving gradient flow analysis and spectral gap estimates on multi-copy operators. It establishes a robust diagnostic tool for characterizing quantum states in quantum information theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental theoretical tools for certifying quantum states, which is crucial for quantum computation and quantum communication protocols that rely on specific state properties.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the problem of determining whether a given quantum state is a bosonic or fermionic Gaussian state, or if it has a bounded overlap with the set of Gaussian states.

**Main result.** The key advancement is proving that a constant number of copies of the state is sufficient to perform this test, overcoming previous results that required the number of copies to scale with the system size (number of modes).

**Method.** The results are derived by analyzing the symmetries of identical copies of Gaussian states and by bounding the distance to the set of Gaussian states using gradient flow techniques and spectral bounds related to random walks.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on bosonic and fermionic Gaussian quantum states, which are central objects in quantum physics and quantum information processing. The analysis involves multi-copy measurements on these states.

**Key observables.** Acceptance probability $p(\psi) = \langle\psi|\otimes 2 P |\psiangle\otimes 2$, and the fidelity $F_G(\psi)$ to the set of Gaussian states.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of copies required for the test, which is shown to be constant, and the spectral gap $\alpha$ of an associated operator $S$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The robustness theorems rely on bounding the spectral gap of a specific three-copy operator $S$, relating the acceptance probability to the fidelity.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the physical implementations of the four distinct tests developed for Gaussianity.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical framework by first establishing the general test using $O(1)$ copies (Theorem 1.1). It then rigorously proves the robustness of this test by analyzing the gradient flow of the acceptance probability, linking it to the spectral gap of the three-copy operator $S$ (Theorem 3.4). Finally, it applies these general results to specific cases like fermionic and bosonic Gaussianity.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Bosonic and fermionic Gaussian quantum states are families of quantum states that play a central role in quantum physics and quantum information processing. We study the problem of testing whether a given state is either Gaussian, or has bounded overlap with any Gaussian state. Previous analyses of this testing problem led to tests that require a number of copies of the state that scales with the number of modes (the system size). In this work we show that a constant number of copies of the state suffices. We derive these results based on the symmetries of identical copies of Gaussian states, and by bounding the distance to the set of Gaussian states through a gradient flow and a spectral bound studied previously for the Kac random walk on a sphere.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proves that the ability to reverse time (i.e., access inverse unitary operations) is a necessary resource for achieving optimal quantum speedups in continuous-time tasks like Hamiltonian property testing. Using a new Fourier-analytic technique, the authors establish lower bounds that demonstrate a clear separation in required evolution time when time reversal is unavailable. This work fundamentally characterizes time reversal as a key resource governing quantum measurement precision.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous establishment of time reversal as a fundamental resource governing quantum measurement precision and algorithm robustness provides deep theoretical insights applicable to open quantum systems and time-dependent dynamics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the fundamental necessity of time reversal (inverse unitary operations) for achieving optimal scaling in continuous-time quantum tasks like Hamiltonian property testing.

**Main result.** It rigorously proves that time reversal is a necessary resource, establishing lower bounds for evolution time that are significantly worse without the ability to reverse time.

**Method.** The authors develop a novel Fourier-analytic approach to quantum lower bounds in continuous time, extending techniques from discrete query models.

**Model / system.** The study analyzes quantum evolution governed by an unknown Hamiltonian H in a continuous-time setting, applied to problems like Hamiltonian certification and locality testing.

**Key observables.** Evolution time (T), error metric (ranging from average-case to worst-case), and the distinguishability of Hamiltonians.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Precision ($\epsilon$), Hilbert space dimension ($d$), and the structure of the Hamiltonian (e.g., local vs. global).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes black-box access to time evolution under the unknown Hamiltonian and relies on establishing separations across a continuous family of error metrics.

**Paper structure.** The work progresses by establishing lower bounds for Hamiltonian certification and locality testing, showing separations between time-reversible and non-time-reversible protocols. It then extends these techniques to provide alternative proofs for the necessity of inverses in amplitude amplification and unstructured search.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum algorithms enable Heisenberg-limited scaling across many tasks in sensing and learning, achieving precision $\varepsilon$ using $O(1/\varepsilon)$ total evolution time. However, in Hamiltonian property testing, the best known algorithms have $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, unless it is possible to $\textit{reverse}$ the flow of time under the Hamiltonian. In this work, we prove that time reversal is necessary to close this gap. We establish evolution time lower bounds for Hamiltonian certification and locality testing, for a continuous family of error metrics ranging from average- to worst-case. We also prove matching upper bounds for Hamiltonian certification in all cases, both with and without time reversal, showing that the advantage from time reversal persists. Our results follow from a new Fourier-analytic approach to quantum lower bounds in continuous time, which is sensitive to time reversal and applicable beyond Hamiltonian property testing. This gives an alternative proof that inverses are required for amplitude amplification and estimation, improving the lower bounds of Tang and Wright and extending to fractional queries. We also show that, for unstructured search, uncertainty in the phase of the oracle destroys the quantum speedup without inverse queries, even when the oracle is fixed and coherent. Our work rigorously establishes time reversal as a resource governing both the precision of quantum measurement and the robustness of quantum algorithms.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously analyzes the query complexity of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms by developing systematic lower-bounding techniques. It proves tight bounds for fundamental problems like phase estimation and search within this model. The work is significant for establishing the theoretical limits of quantum computation when measurements force classical processing between quantum steps.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous, systematic tools for establishing quantum lower bounds in a model that bridges quantum computation with classical information processing, which is highly relevant for understanding practical quantum advantage.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper studies the query complexity of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, where computation is broken into short quantum subroutines separated by classical measurements.

**Main result.** They establish tight, optimal upper and lower bounds for several problems, including phase estimation, amplitude estimation, search, and the AND-OR tree, in this hybrid model.

**Method.** The authors develop systematic frameworks for proving lower bounds by analyzing probability distributions over measurement transcripts and bounding a 'progress measure' that quantifies distinguishability between input states.

**Model / system.** The model is the hybrid quantum-classical query model, where quantum computation is restricted to subroutines making at most $q$ oracle queries, followed by measurement and classical processing.

**Key observables.** The primary observables are the required number of queries, the target precision ($\epsilon$), and the statistical distance (e.g., Hellinger distance) between distributions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Key parameters include the maximum queries per block ($q$), the search size ($N$), and the dimensions of the AND-OR tree ($m, n$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The lower bounds are proven to be optimal up to a constant factor for all $q \ge 1$. The analysis relies on bounding progress measures derived from measurement transcripts.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the hybrid query model, develops a general framework using progress measures for lower bounds, and then applies this framework to derive specific bounds for phase estimation, amplitude estimation, search, and the AND-OR tree.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study hybrid quantum-classical algorithms in the query model. The computation consists of quantum subroutines that make at most $q$ oracle queries; between subroutines, all qubits are measured and discarded. We prove matching upper and lower bounds for several problems in this model:   (i) (Unbiased) Phase estimation up to a precision $ε$ requires $Θ(\frac{1}{q ε^2})$ queries;   (ii) (Unbiased) Amplitude estimation up to a precision $ε$ requires $Θ(\frac{p(1-p)}{q ε^2})$ queries;   (iii) Search among $N$ items requires $Θ(\frac{N}{q})$ queries;   (iv) Two level AND-OR tree (AND of $m$ ORs, with $n$ inputs to each OR) requires $Θ(\frac{nm}{q})$ queries.   All of these bounds are optimal up to a constant factor, for all $q$ from 1, corresponding to the classical complexity, to $Q(f)$, the unrestricted quantum query complexity of the respective problem. We also derive a hybrid lower bound for distinguishing two distributions specified by a state-preparation unitary; this bound is tight up to a logarithmic factor.   Besides specific lower bounds, an important contribution is developing methods for proving lower bounds on hybrid quantum algorithms (which have been very ad-hoc up to now). The first two bounds follow from a common framework: we analyze probability distributions over measurement transcripts and bound a progress measure that captures their distinguishability. The AND-OR bound requires a more delicate argument, combining two progress measures that track the information available to the algorithm classically and in quantum form, respectively.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops lower bounds for quantum sampling by analyzing the Linear Cross-Entropy Benchmark (XEB) score. It proves that achieving a constant advantage over the ideal score requires a super-polynomial number of queries, specifically $\Omega(N^{1/3})$. This work provides a strong theoretical link between measurement performance and the amount of certified randomness extractable from a quantum device.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on complexity theory, the rigorous quantification of certified randomness from limited quantum measurements is fundamental to understanding the practical limits of quantum advantage demonstrations.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates what a high Linear Cross-Entropy Benchmark (XEB) score certifies about an untrusted quantum device performing random circuit sampling.

**Main result.** It establishes that exceeding the ideal score by a constant requires $\Omega(N^{1/3})$ queries for Haar and Fourier ensembles, and that near-ideal scores certify $n - O(\log n)$ bits of smooth min-entropy.

**Method.** The analysis employs quantum query models, utilizing progress measures (like norms of coherent amplitudes or expansions in orthogonal polynomials) to derive lower bounds on query complexity.

**Model / system.** The study is set in the quantum query model, analyzing random circuit sampling using oracles drawn from the Haar ensemble or the Fourier ensemble.

**Key observables.** The XEB score, smooth min-entropy, and the progress measure quantifying the excess over the ideal score.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of outcomes $N$, the number of queries $q$, and the constant advantage $\epsilon$ over the ideal score.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the query model framework and the ability to construct progress measures that are zero for the honest sampler.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the expected scores for Haar-random states versus the number of queries, comparing the honest sampler to the squaring algorithm. Table 1 compares query complexity bounds for achieving specific score advantages.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops lower bounds by analyzing progress measures related to the excess score, first for the Haar and Fourier ensembles, and then applies these bounds to quantify the certified randomness achievable.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Random circuit sampling experiments, the leading demonstrations of quantum computational advantage, are tested with the linear cross-entropy benchmark (XEB), which scores outcomes by their ideal probabilities. We study what a high XEB score certifies about an untrusted quantum device. In the quantum query model, we show that the honest sampler's ideal score acts as a Tsirelson bound for efficient devices and certified randomness. First, exceeding the ideal score by a constant requires $Ω(N^{1/3})$ queries for the Haar and Fourier oracle ensembles with $N$ outcomes, and this bound is tight; this proves an earlier conjecture for Haar-random states and extends it to Fourier sampling. Second, for Fourier sampling and for Haar-random states accessed through the canonical state-preparation oracle, the $n$-bit output of a device that makes polynomially many queries and scores within $o(1)$ of the ideal score has $n-O(\log n)$ bits of smooth min-entropy, even against an adversary who is entangled with the device and later learns the oracle; this is nearly optimal. As a corollary, sampling the collision distribution, which is proportional to the square of the ideal distribution, has query complexity $Θ(N^{1/3})$, and a coherent version of the same algorithm approximately prepares quantum Hadamard products of states with uniform amplitude magnitudes. Both lower bounds rest on progress measures that bound the excess over the ideal score and increase only slightly with each query. For Fourier sampling the measure is the norm of the coherent amplitudes for removing pairs in a purification of the random function, combining the polynomial method with the compressed oracle technique; for Haar-random states it is the square root of the average level in an expansion in Dirichlet orthogonal polynomials, controlled by an exact identity for the effect of one observation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the theoretical question of whether intermediate measurements are necessary in quantum computation when operating under limited resources like logarithmic space. The authors prove that for standard gate sets, measurements can be eliminated while maintaining computational power, extending known techniques to general channels and quantum verification settings.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides deep theoretical insights into the resource requirements of quantum computation, particularly concerning the necessity of intermediate measurements, which is fundamental for designing efficient quantum algorithms.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is determining if intermediate measurements in quantum computation can be eliminated while preserving computational power, specifically addressing the one-sided error case ($	ext{RQL} = 	ext{RQUL}$).

**Main result.** The authors prove that $	ext{RQL}_{\Gamma} = 	ext{RQUL}_{\Gamma}$ for the standard gate set $\Gamma$, preserving polynomial time, logarithmic space, and zero acceptance on no-instances.

**Method.** The proof extends the density-matrix doubling method to general channels and utilizes a history-checking construction for quantum verification.

**Model / system.** The work analyzes quantum computation models ($	ext{RQL}$, $	ext{RQUL}$) operating in polynomial time with logarithmic space, using gate sets like $\Gamma = \{	ext{H}, 	ext{T}, 	ext{CNOT}\}$ as the underlying computational resource.

**Key observables.** Acceptance probability (must be exactly zero on no-instances), computational space ($	ext{O}(\log n)$), and time complexity (polynomial).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The error type (two-sided vs. one-sided) and the specific gate set $\Gamma$ or $	ext{G}$ used for the computation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof relies on the established two-sided measurement-elimination theorem and assumes specific conditions on the gate sets (e.g., exact inverses or entries in a fixed CM field).

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 summarizes prior complexity results; Figure 2 details the direct simulation process involving reweighting and unitary circuits; Figure 3 illustrates the factorization of the simulation into algebraic and unitary components.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the core measurement elimination result ($	ext{RQL} = 	ext{RQUL}$), then detailing the simulation construction using reweighting and unitary circuits, and finally extending these results to broader gate sets and quantum verification settings.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Intermediate measurements let quantum computations discard information and reuse their workspace. Deferring all measurements can require storing their entire history, which need not preserve logarithmic space. Fefferman and Remscrim proved that measurements can nevertheless be eliminated with two-sided bounded error, and asked whether the same holds with one-sided error [FR21]. We prove RQLΓ = RQULΓ for the standard gate set Γ = {H, T, CNOT}, preserving polynomial time, logarithmic space, and exactly zero acceptance on no-instances. Our proof extends the density-matrix doubling method of Girish, Raz and Zhan [ GRZ21 ] to general channels, including resets and classical memory. We also prove measurement elimination for broader finite gate sets with exact inverses, including suitable gates with transcendental entries, and establish gate-set independence for a specified family of algebraic gate sets. A separate history-checking construction proves QMAL1,G = QUMAL1,G under explicit gate assumptions: measurements can also be eliminated from logarithmic-space quantum verification while preserving perfect completeness

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the randomness generated in quantum systems evolving via dual-unitary circuits when measurements are performed on a portion of the system. It rigorously establishes that the projected state ensemble approximates a quantum state k-design using only a bath of polynomial size relative to k. The methodology introduces a defect-transport picture to quantify this convergence rate, which is crucial for understanding finite-size effects in quantum thermalization.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, quantitative tool for understanding how local unitary dynamics generate complex, highly mixed states (like k-designs) in finite quantum systems, bridging quantum information theory with statistical physics concepts of thermalization.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the rate of convergence of projected quantum state ensembles, generated by dual-unitary circuits, towards a quantum state k-design at finite bath sizes.

**Main result.** It rigorously proves that under specific assumptions, a bath of polynomial size suffices to approximate k-designs, establishing a finite-size convergence rate.

**Method.** The authors develop a microscopic transport interpretation of emergent randomness, reformulating the convergence problem using a transfer matrix approach in a space-time flipped picture.

**Model / system.** The model involves quantum evolution governed by dual-unitary brickwork circuits, partitioning the system into an unmeasured subsystem (A) and a measured bath subsystem (B).

**Key observables.** The primary observable is the projected ensemble's k-th moment, $ho^{(k)}_{	ext{EA}}$, which is compared against the Haar random ensemble's k-moment.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The key parameters include the target moment order $k$ and the finite bath size $N_B$, with the result showing scaling as $	ext{poly}(k)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof relies on three quantitative assumptions: local permutation mixing, a bound on recurrent backward motion, and contraction at the measured boundary.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the structure of the k-fold dual-unitary brickwork circuit and the diagrammatic representation of the transfer matrix used to track moment evolution.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining dual-unitarity and folded circuits, to developing the defect-transport mechanism for convergence, and finally providing rigorous finite-replica treatments for normalization.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the emergent randomness in projected ensembles generated by dual-unitary circuits. Specifically, we consider evolution by solvable dual-unitary brickwork circuits followed by measurements on part of the system, which induce an ensemble of states on the unmeasured subsystem. Previous work has established that this projected ensemble of states forms a quantum state design in the limit where the bath size is large, but the rate of convergence at finite bath size has not been rigorously established. Under three inverse-polynomial assumptions, local permutation mixing, a bound on recurrent backward motion, and contraction at the measured boundary, we fill this gap and prove that a bath of polynomial size suffices to form approximate $k$-designs. In establishing our results, we develop a microscopic transport interpretation of emergent randomness in the projected ensemble, in which deviations from local permutation operators appear as defects, and make connections with the theory of quantum walks.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory for active matter, treating collective motion as 'perceptual matter' derived from neural models. It successfully bridges the gap between individual agent perception and macroscopic continuum behavior by deriving stability criteria and transport equations. The work is significant for showing how specific sensory and decision mechanisms dictate collective instabilities and flow patterns.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on active matter, the rigorous derivation of macroscopic equations from underlying microscopic rules, coupled with stability analysis, shares methodological parallels with non-equilibrium statistical mechanics used in quantum many-body systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To derive a nonlocal kinetic and hydrodynamic theory connecting neural representations (from Harmonic Theory) to macroscopic collective material behavior without assuming explicit heading alignment.

**Main result.** The theory predicts a torque-driven density instability and successfully links macroscopic continuum coefficients to microscopic sensory and decision-making factors.

**Method.** The authors derive the continuum theory by applying closure approximations and moment expansions to the particle-level stochastic differential equation derived from the Harmonic Theory particle law.

**Model / system.** The system models 'perceptual matter'—the collective motion of agents whose turning behavior is governed by how their neural representations of neighbors' bearings and distances influence their movement.

**Key observables.** Density ($ho$), polarization ($f_1$), and the eigenvalues ($\lambda$) derived from linear stability analysis.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Perceptual channels ($q_n$), sensory acuity ($c_n(\sigma)$), decision dynamics ($M_n(W)$), and interaction distance ($J(r)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions include the molecular chaos closure approximation and the rapid relaxation of the decision bump relative to sensory changes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the scale-by-scale route from perception to material dynamics, connecting perceptual harmonic coefficients to continuum transport equations.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from the microscopic particle law (SDE) to a kinetic field description, then uses moment expansion and Fourier transforms to derive the macroscopic, closed hydrodynamic equations, culminating in a linear stability analysis.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

How do neural representations of neighbors become collective material behavior? Harmonic Theory (HT) reduces bearing representations to signed perceptual channels traceable to sensory acuity, decision dynamics, and interaction distance. Here we derive a nonlocal kinetic and hydrodynamic theory from the HT particle law without introducing heading alignment. The resulting fields retain HT's order-resolved perceptual spectrum and keep the neural and sensory origin of each coefficient visible. The theory predicts a torque-driven density instability: HT's direct-approach channel turns agents toward density excesses, while self-propulsion carries them inward. For isotropic spatial interactions and positive rotational diffusion, perceptual channel $n$ generically first affects conserved density at spatial order $k^{2n}$, and the full radial transforms select finite pattern wavelengths. Two populations can share the same long-wave instability threshold yet select different initial pattern spacings because their higher perceptual channels differ. Beyond onset, the one-particle continuum sustains a bidirectional nematic column; a prescribed, symmetry-allowed two-stream response amplifies a directional imbalance into sustained polar flow. In a distinct pure-repulsion regime, one-particle calculations show polar transport and translating transverse bands, with late pattern selection sensitive to numerical transport. The framework connects neural and sensory mechanisms to continuum coefficients, instabilities, and alignment-free collective motion.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work quantifies how cavity dissipation degrades the predicted energy splitting (Rabi splitting) in strongly coupled light-matter systems compared to ideal models. By modifying the Hamiltonian to account for finite cavity quality factors, the authors show that losses are a major factor, necessitating their inclusion in advanced ab-initio simulations for accurate quantum control protocols.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it provides a necessary, computationally feasible correction to standard QED models, ensuring that theoretical predictions accurately reflect experimental realities involving cavity losses.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the limitation of assuming ideal, lossless cavities in Cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (Cavity-QED) by quantifying the effect of cavity dissipation on light-matter strong coupling.

**Main result.** Cavity dissipation significantly reduces the Rabi splitting by over 20% for realistic quality factors, demonstrating that losses substantially modify polaritonic energetics.

**Method.** The authors extend the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian by incorporating dissipation via a damped harmonic oscillator model, leading to a time-averaged, Hermitian Hamiltonian suitable for ab-initio QED methods.

**Model / system.** The system involves light-matter interaction within a Fabry-Pérot cavity, modeled using the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian extended to include cavity damping ($\kappa = \omega_k/Q$).

**Key observables.** Rabi splitting and polaritonic energetics.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cavity Quality Factor (Q), coupling strength ($\lambda$), and the strong-coupling regime.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the very weak damping approximation and a first-order Maclaurin expansion of the vector potential.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 shows the polaritonic state dispersion of p-nitroaniline in a lossy Fabry-Pérot cavity.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the modified Hamiltonian, details the mathematical transformation (PZW transformation) to maintain a real-valued, Hermitian form, and applies this framework to calculate the spectral changes using QED-CCSD.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (Cavity-QED) offers a powerful framework for controlling light-matter interactions, yet first-principles approaches commonly assume ideal, lossless cavity fields. Here, we introduce a minimal extension to the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian that accounts for cavity dissipation through the experimentally accessible cavity quality factor Q. The electromagnetic field is described as a damped harmonic oscillator within the very weak damping approximation. In this framework, cavity losses only enter the light-matter interaction and dipole self-energy terms, without introducing additional photonic degrees of freedom. A time-dependent unitary transformation yields a real-valued Hermitian Hamiltonian that can be incorporated into existing ab-initio QED methods without additional computational cost or changes in scaling. We combined the approach to the QED-CCSD method and investigated the effects of cavity dissipation on the optical spectrum of a p-nitroaniline molecule under strong light-matter coupling. We found that, for realistic quality factors, cavity dissipation can reduce the Rabi splitting by more than 20% compared to the ideal-cavity limit, even though the system remains in the strong-coupling regime. Convergence towards the ideal-cavity limit then requires substantially higher quality factors than those needed to establish strong coupling. These results demonstrate that cavity dissipation can significantly affect polaritonic energetics and highlight the importance of incorporating experimentally realistic cavity losses into quantitative ab-initio Cavity-QED simulations to accurately guide experimental protocols.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops HAMLET, a geometric framework that models machine learning optimization as a dissipative dynamical system. It treats the loss as potential energy and the parameter metric as kinetic geometry, deriving a full mechanical description. By analyzing controlled examples, the authors demonstrate how the metric induces a geometric force, providing a unified, physically rigorous view of optimization.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between geometric dynamics (Hamiltonian mechanics) and the optimization landscape provides a powerful, physically grounded lens for understanding deep learning training dynamics, which is relevant to understanding complex energy landscapes in many-body physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper reframes machine learning parameter optimization from standard iterative rules into the framework of a dissipative dynamical system.

**Main result.** The proposed HAMLET framework successfully models optimization as a mechanical process governed by a Hamiltonian, a geometric force derived from the metric, and a dissipation term.

**Method.** The authors derive the dynamics from a variational principle, leading to a continuous system that satisfies a monotonic energy-dissipation relation.

**Model / system.** The model treats model parameters as generalized coordinates, the loss function as potential energy, and a positive-definite metric defining the local kinetic geometry of the parameter space.

**Key observables.** Poincaré return maps, geometric force ($F_{geo}$), energy dissipation rate, and mean test accuracy/negative log-likelihood on benchmarks.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The metric tensor $g(	heta)$, the loss function $L(	heta)$, and the dissipation coefficient $\gamma$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is that optimization can be viewed as the trajectory of a physically motivated dynamical system, requiring the metric and loss to be sufficiently smooth.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare Poincaré analysis for pixel space (constant metric) versus MPS space (position-dependent metric), showing how the geometric force and metric variation affect phase-space contraction.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the Hamiltonian/dissipative framework, derives the governing equations including the geometric force, illustrates this with controlled image reconstruction problems (pixel vs. MPS), and concludes with benchmark testing on MNIST.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Optimization in machine learning is usually expressed through iterative rules that update model parameters using information from the loss landscape. In this work, we study an alternative viewpoint in which parameter optimization is treated as the evolution of a dissipative dynamical system. The model parameters are regarded as generalized coordinates, the loss acts as a potential energy, and a positive-definite metric defines the local kinetic geometry of parameter space. Starting from a variational formulation, we derive the corresponding Hamiltonian dynamics, the geometric force generated by a position-dependent metric, and a metric-compatible Rayleigh dissipation law. The resulting continuous system satisfies a monotonic energy-dissipation relation, while its discrete form allows the influence of curvature on the optimization trajectory to be studied directly. We illustrate the framework using a controlled CIFAR-10 image-reconstruction problem for which the optimum is known analytically. With the image Hessian used as the metric, the curvature dependence of the quadratic modal dynamics is removed. We then reparameterize the same image as a matrix product state, producing a genuinely position-dependent metric and a nonzero geometric force. Poincaré return maps provide a complementary phase-space view of the resulting contraction dynamics. These examples establish HAMLET as a geometric, energy-based framework for studying optimization as dissipative motion in parameter space. On a five-seed MNIST MLP benchmark, HAMLET attains the highest mean test accuracy (97.95\%) and the lowest mean test negative log-likelihood (0.0696) among the three evaluated optimizers.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses time-resolved THG spectroscopy to study how excitons behave in high-purity silicon under non-equilibrium, non-thermal conditions at room temperature. By analyzing the nonlinear response, the authors successfully distinguish the characteristic dynamics of excitons from those of free electron-hole plasma. This demonstrates a powerful tool for probing strongly correlated many-body physics in semiconductors.

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to spectroscopically isolate and characterize non-equilibrium excitonic correlations using nonlinear optical techniques provides insights into strongly correlated electron behavior in semiconductors, bridging concepts from excitonic insulators and plasma physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the nonthermal nonlinear many-body excitonic dynamics occurring in high-purity silicon at room temperature.

**Main result.** The research successfully distinguishes between plasma-driven and exciton-driven nonlinear responses, showing that excitonic dynamics exhibit a non-linear power-law dependence on the THz drive field, unlike the linear plasma response.

**Method.** Time-resolved optical pump-terahertz third-harmonic generation (THG) spectroscopy was employed to probe the ultrafast, non-equilibrium charge dynamics.

**Model / system.** The physical system is high-purity silicon, an indirect bandgap semiconductor. The dynamics are studied far from thermal equilibrium using pulsed optical pumping, allowing the observation of transient excitonic states.

**Key observables.** Third-harmonic generation (THG) signal, separated into plasma ($	ext{(3f)}_P$) and excitonic ($	ext{(3f)}_E$) contributions; THG intensity dependence on THz drive fluence ($I_f$) and optical pump fluence ($I_{op}$); time-delay dependence ($t_{pd}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Picosecond time scale; Room temperature (where excitons are unstable in equilibrium); Non-linear dependence ($I_{3f} \propto I_f^{2.9 \pm 0.1}$) for excitons.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the observed differences in fluence dependence are characteristic of the underlying physical processes (plasma vs. exciton).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate time-domain THz third-harmonic amplitudes and integrated intensity dependence on THz drive fluence, clearly separating the plasma and excitonic contributions based on their nonlinear scaling and time evolution.

**Paper structure.** The paper presents experimental results derived from time-resolved THG spectroscopy, systematically analyzing the dependence of the signal on pump-drive delay, THz drive fluence, and optical pump fluence to differentiate between plasma and excitonic nonlinear responses.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We report time-resolved optical pump-terahertz third-harmonic generation spectroscopy of picosecond nonthermal many-body charge dynamics in high-purity silicon at room temperature. Although in thermal equilibrium excitons in silicon are unstable due to a lower binding energy than the thermal energy at room temperature, following pulsed non-resonant optical pumping we can identify the formation of transient excitonic states on the picosecond time scale in our high-resolution nonlinear spectroscopic measurements. In contrast to unbound electron-hole pairs, the nonthermal many-body excitonic dynamics feature a characteristic time-dependent evolution, a distinct dependence on charge density, and a nonperturbative nonlinear terahertz response.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the stability and motion of clusters of magnetic bimerons, which are topological magnetic textures. Using advanced computational methods, the authors determine that the cluster's dynamics are constrained to move along an ellipse in velocity space. This provides a quantitative understanding of how topological charge and applied currents govern the collective behavior of these magnetic structures.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical micromagnetics, the study of topological defects and their collective dynamics under external driving forces (currents) shares conceptual links with understanding emergent collective excitations in strongly correlated electron systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the stability and current-driven dynamics of bimeron clusters, which are magnetic skyrmion-like structures with mixed topological indices.

**Main result.** The cluster's velocity space is found to be an ellipse governed by the model Hamiltonian, and the stability is determined by energy barriers associated with separation, interchange, and annihilation.

**Method.** The authors employed the Geodesic Nudged Elastic Band (GNEB) method for stability analysis and the Thiele approach for analyzing steady-state dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system involves magnetic bimerons (in-plane skyrmions) governed by a micromagnetic Hamiltonian and dynamics described by the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) equation, incorporating Zhang-Li and Slonczewski torques.

**Key observables.** Topological charge (Q), energy barriers for transitions (separation, interchange, annihilation), and the elliptical geometry of the cluster velocity vector (v).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The total topological charge (Q), damping ($\alpha$), and the specific forms of the applied currents (Zhang-Li vs. Slonczewski).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the rigid motion approximation inherent in the Thiele approach, and the annihilation transition is considered irrelevant at low current strengths.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the bimeron/antibimeron structures and stable clusters, show the minimum energy path (MEP) transitions, and map the resulting velocity space as ellipses for different current driving mechanisms.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by first analyzing the stability of the simplest bimeron-antibimeron pair using GNEB, establishing general principles. It then moves to studying the dynamics under applied currents using the Thiele approach, culminating in the derivation and analysis of the elliptical velocity manifold.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we study bimerons (in-plane skyrmions) and their clusters composed of states with mixed topological indices. These clusters provide flexibility in controlling the skyrmion Hall angle, which depends on the cluster's total topological charge. First, using the simplest such cluster, a bimeron-antibimeron pair, we examine its stability with the geodesic nudged elastic band method and identify three mechanisms -- bimeron separation, interchange, and annihilation -- with comparable energy barriers that determine the pair's overall stability. This provides an upper bound for the stability of more sophisticated clusters of bimerons and antibimerons. Then, we numerically study the clusters' dynamics for currents applied in-plane and perpendicular to the plane, corresponding to the Zhang-Li and Slonczewski mechanisms. Finally, we analyze the dynamics of a wide variety of bimeron clusters within the Thiele approach and show that their velocities always lie on a specific ellipse whose parameters are fully governed by the model Hamiltonian.

</details>

**Summary.** This work simulates and analyzes the noise effects on CMOS analog spiking neurons, demonstrating that time-varying inputs improve spike timing reliability compared to constant inputs. By applying stochastic thermodynamics, the authors establish a fundamental physical limit (the TUR) that governs the trade-off between signal precision and energy dissipation in these artificial systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The application of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics tools like the TUR to analyze the operational limits of artificial neural circuits provides a powerful, physics-grounded constraint on computational efficiency and reliability.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the fundamental interplay between noise and excitability in analog spiking neurons, specifically analyzing how input stimuli affect the reliability and jitter of spike timing.

**Main result.** Time-varying inputs significantly reduce spike time jitter compared to constant excitation, and the analysis uses the Stochastic Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation (TUR) to establish a fundamental reliability-dissipation tradeoff.

**Method.** The study employs industrial physics-based transient noise SPICE simulations combined with theoretical tools from stochastic thermodynamics, such as the TUR.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a CMOS analog spiking neuron modeled after the Morris-Lecar system, designed for neuromorphic hardware. The analysis compares its behavior under constant vs. time-varying external stimuli.

**Key observables.** Spike time jitter (phase noise), spike time reliability, dissipated energy ($E_{	ext{dissip}}$), and the empirical frequency ($N/t$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Constant vs. time-varying input current, temperature ($kT$), and the fundamental limit set by the TUR.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the applicability of stochastic thermodynamics principles, though it notes the TUR may not apply to the non-stationary excitability regime.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the CMOS neuron's operation in both oscillatory (high jitter) and excitability (low jitter) regimes under different input currents, alongside plots comparing accumulated jitter over time.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from simulating the physical behavior of the neuron under different noise conditions, quantifying jitter accumulation, and culminating in a theoretical analysis using the TUR to place fundamental limits on the achievable precision.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A spiking neuron is a dynamical system exhibiting a limit cycle (a spike) when subject to sufficiently excitatory input. Famous neuroscience experiments by Bryant and Segundo as well as Mainen and Sejnowski revealed that the spike times of some biological neurons are more reliable when subject to time-varying stimuli compared to constant ones. Provided with an industrial physics-based transient noise SPICE simulation framework compatible with foundry transistor compact models, we have demonstrated similar behaviours for a CMOS analog spiking neuron designed for neuromorphic computing hardware platforms. Under constant excitation current, the neuron operates in oscillatory regime and the empirical periods (interspike intervals) suffer from accumulated phase noise (jitter) during successive cycles, mainly due to the thermal noise of transistors. A time-varying input is reported to be capable of triggering output spikes according to a controlled statetransition mechanism, thereby significantly reducing the spike time jitter in the excitability regime. The physical limitation of the oscillatory or rate-coding regime in terms of reliabilitydissipation tradeoff is further evidenced by a stochastic thermodynamic uncertainty relation, a theorem that applies to general overdamped dissipative stochastic dynamical systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a joint GKP encoding scheme to protect GHZ states transmitted through noisy bosonic quantum channels. By optimizing the lattice structure based on channel information, the authors show that joint processing adapts to anisotropic noise better than simpler product methods. This advances the understanding of robust quantum communication in complex, realistic quantum network environments.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete, advanced framework for quantum communication over realistic noisy channels, directly addressing resource limitations (like CSI) in quantum networking protocols.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the challenge of transmitting fragile Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states over realistic, nonunitary Quantum Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (QuMIMO) bosonic channels.

**Main result.** Joint GKP lattice shaping significantly outperforms product GKP processing, demonstrating that adapting the logical lattice to the anisotropic noise geometry is crucial for high-fidelity state preservation.

**Method.** The authors employ a sophisticated transceiver combining programmable passive meshes, quantum-limited MMSE gain, local GKP recovery, and joint classical syndrome decoding.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as a bosonic QuMIMO channel governed by a coupled-mode Gaussian evolution equation, incorporating coherent mixing, mode-dependent attenuation, and Gaussian noise.

**Key observables.** GHZ-state fidelity ($F_{GHZ}$), entanglement fidelity ($	ext{Fe}$), and coherent information ($I_c$) are used to quantify state preservation.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Channel-State Information (CSI) availability (full instantaneous vs. singular-value conditioned vs. statistical) and the degree of coherent basis drift are critical parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The required CSI is assumed to be supplied by an offline channel-estimation stage, and the exact classical Pauli-coset decoding is complex, necessitating structured lattices.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the CSI-aware Gaussian QuMIMO-GKP architecture and show performance metrics (like $F_{GHZ}$) across varying propagation distances, comparing joint vs. product processing schemes.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the physical model, introduces the GKP encoding/decoding framework, develops optimization functionals based on residual Pauli distributions, and compares performance across different CSI utilization regimes.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study transmission of a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state over nonunitary quantum multiple-input multiple-output (QuMIMO) channels using finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoding. A coupled-mode model describes coherent mixing, mode-dependent attenuation, and Gaussian noise. The transceiver combines programmable passive meshes, quantum-limited MMSE gain, local GKP recovery, and joint classical syndrome decoding. We optimize complex-Givens lattices using instantaneous channel-state information (CSI), current singular values with channel statistics, or statistics alone. Simulations show that joint lattice shaping outperforms product GKP processing. Under coherent-basis drift, full instantaneous CSI improves GHZ-state preservation, whereas singular-value conditioned and fully statistical designs perform similarly because neither resolves the current singular frames. These findings identify singular-frame geometry as a critical resource beyond attenuation knowledge where joint GKP processing adapts the logical lattice and receiver to anisotropic bosonic noise rather than merely inverting multimode mixing.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates spontaneous U(1) symmetry breaking in 1D quantum spin chains, contradicting standard expectations for such systems. By applying advanced numerical simulations and field theory, the authors locate an interacting quantum critical point, yielding critical exponents that deviate from simple theoretical predictions. This establishes a new criterion for understanding symmetry breaking in low-dimensional quantum materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The finding of $z < 2$ provides a concrete, measurable criterion to distinguish novel mechanisms of continuous symmetry breaking in low-dimensional quantum systems, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum criticality in condensed matter systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the spontaneous breaking of U(1) spin-rotation symmetry and the emergence of an interacting quantum critical point in 1+1 dimensions, challenging expectations from the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorem.

**Main result.** The study finds numerical evidence for interacting quantum critical behavior, determining the correlation-length critical exponent $\nu \approx 0.60$ and a dynamical critical exponent $z < 2$, which implies a mechanism for symmetry breaking distinct from frustration-free models.

**Method.** The research employs a combination of numerical techniques, including Subsystem Binder scaling and DMRG/VUMPS simulations, alongside field-theoretic renormalization group (RG) analysis.

**Model / system.** The models studied are lattice spin-1/2 and spin-1 chains with finite-range interactions, analyzed via their continuum field theory description involving a U(1) phase field $\theta$.

**Key observables.** Correlation-length critical exponent ($\nu$), dynamical critical exponent ($z$), and the finite-size scaling of the transverse magnetization ($\langle m_{\perp}^2 \rangle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The critical couplings ($g_{1c}$) and the comparison of calculated exponents ($\nu \neq 0.5$, $z \neq 2$) against Gaussian predictions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the validity of continuum field theories and the applicability of finite-size scaling methods to locate the critical point.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the half-chain Binder ratio crossing point analysis to estimate critical couplings and exponents, and show the finite-size scaling of the transverse magnetization density.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical conflict with the Mermin-Wagner theorem, then develops the field-theoretic action, applies RG analysis, and finally uses advanced numerical methods (DMRG/VUMPS) on specific spin chains to extract universal critical exponents.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorem motivates the expectation that continuous symmetries remain unbroken in one-dimensional quantum ground states. Here, contrary to this expectation, we demonstrate the spontaneous breaking of U(1) spin-rotation symmetry and the emergence of an interacting quantum critical point in lattice spin-$1/2$ and spin-$1$ chains. Using subsystem Binder scaling, we locate the critical point and determine the correlation-length critical exponent as $ν= 0.60 \pm 0.02$, distinct from the Gaussian value $0.5$ but consistent with the perturbative renormalization-group prediction. We further analyze the finite-size scaling of the lowest neutral excitation gap and obtain the dynamical critical exponent $z=1.986 \pm 0.005$. The result $z < 2$ is incompatible with microscopic realizations of this critical theory by frustration-free models, implying a mechanism for continuous symmetry breaking in one-dimensional quantum ground states distinct from frustration freeness.

</details>
