**Summary.** This paper characterizes when all gates in the Clifford hierarchy for a single qudit are semi-Clifford, proving this holds if and only if the qudit dimension $d$ is square-free. It develops sophisticated mathematical tools using module theory to distinguish between various gate classes ($	ext{SC}, 	ext{LSC}, 	ext{N}, 	ext{GSC}$) in composite dimensions.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides deep structural constraints on quantum gates, which is fundamental for understanding resource-efficient quantum computation protocols like gate teleportation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the necessary and sufficient conditions for all gates in the Clifford hierarchy of a single qudit to be semi-Clifford, particularly when the qudit dimension $d$ is composite.

**Main result.** The hierarchy gates are semi-Clifford if and only if the dimension $d$ is square-free; otherwise, various structural equivalences between gate classes (SC, LSC, N, GSC) fail.

**Method.** The authors extend results from prime dimensions to composite dimensions using advanced ring-theoretic tools, module theory over $\mathbb{Z}_d$, and analysis of symplectic modules.

**Model / system.** The system is a single qudit of dimension $d$, whose underlying mathematical structure is analyzed using the symplectic module $\mathbb{Z}_d^2$. The analysis involves classifying various types of quantum gates (Clifford, Semi-Clifford, etc.).

**Key observables.** The membership of gates in different structural classes ($	ext{SC}, 	ext{LSC}, 	ext{N}, 	ext{GSC}$) and the square-free nature of the dimension $d$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension $d$ (especially its prime factorization), and the level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy ($C_k$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis requires using ring-theoretic substitutes for vector-space methods, which is necessary when $d$ is composite.

**Figures summary.** Figures summarize the relationships between the four types of gates ($	ext{SC}, 	ext{N}, 	ext{LSC}, 	ext{GSC}$) across different dimensions and hierarchy levels.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the main theorem relating semi-Clifford property to square-free dimensions. It then delves into the mathematical machinery by analyzing Lagrangian submodules of the symplectic module $\mathbb{Z}_{2p^\alpha}^2$ to support the structural claims regarding gate equivalences.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

An important question in quantum information theory asks whether every gate in the Clifford hierarchy is semi-Clifford or not, as such gates admit resource-efficient implementations via gate teleportation. Extending recent results for prime dimensions~\cite{silva_clifford_2025}, we prove that every hierarchy gate on a single qudit of dimension \(d\) is semi-Clifford, if and only if \(d\) is square-free. In composite dimensions, \(\mathbb{Z}_d^2\) is a symplectic module rather than a vector space, motivating a distinction between four types of gates. Semi-Clifford gates ($\mathcal{SC}$) are the ones that become diagonal under left and right multiplication by Clifford gates, while a broader class $\mathcal{N}$ admits a permutation diagonal form, under left and right multiplication by Cliffords. Lagrangian semi-Clifford gates ($\mathcal{LSC}$) conjugate some maximal abelian Pauli subgroup to another, whereas generalized semi-Clifford gates ($\mathcal{GSC}$) map some maximal abelian Pauli subalgebra to another under conjugation. In square-free dimensions, we have \(\mathcal{SC}=\mathcal{LSC}\) and \(\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{GSC}\), but when \(d\) is not square-free, these equivalences can fail, as Lagrangian submodules can become non-free. We also show that every third-level gate of the one-qudit Clifford hierarchy is a generalized semi-Clifford in arbitrary dimensions.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel, non-sampling predictor to calculate the leading term of the Logical Error Rate (LER) for Quantum Error Correcting codes. It overcomes the exponential computational barrier faced by traditional Monte Carlo methods, allowing for the efficient analysis of complex, deeply concatenated quantum codes. This tool is crucial for assessing the fault-tolerance limits of quantum computation.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on abstract QEC theory, the development of efficient, non-sampling analytical tools for error rate prediction is highly relevant to simulating complex quantum hardware noise models in AMO and quantum optics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is the computational intractability of estimating the Logical Error Rate (LER) for Quantum Error Correcting (QEC) codes, especially highly concatenated ones, using standard Monte Carlo sampling.

**Main result.** The authors propose a novel, non-sampling predictor that computes the leading monomial of the LER as a polynomial in the physical error rate $p$, achieving polynomial time complexity in code parameters and linear in the concatenation level $\ell$.

**Method.** The method involves deriving the leading term of the LER polynomial by analyzing the structure of error classes and utilizing a recursive approach for concatenated codes, avoiding explicit sampling.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is quantum computation protected by QEC codes, where errors are assumed to be independent Pauli errors on physical qubits. The complexity scales with the code distance $d$ and the number of concatenation levels $\ell$.

**Key observables.** Logical Error Rate (LER), the leading monomial $c p^o$ of the LER polynomial, and class likelihoods $W_\lambda(s)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Physical error rate ($p$), code distance ($d$), number of concatenation levels ($\ell$), and relative error ($\varepsilon$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The predictor is proven exact for unconcatenated codes; for concatenated codes, the recursive approach is an approximation of the exact exponential-time computation.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the exponential scaling of required Monte Carlo shots versus code distance. Figure 1(b) compares the wall-clock time of various LER estimation methods, showing the predictor's efficiency.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of Monte Carlo sampling for LER. It then introduces the predictor, proving its exactness for unconcatenated codes. For concatenated codes, it develops a recursive approximation and validates it against exact enumeration for various code types.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Estimating the logical error rate (LER) of a quantum error-correcting (QEC) code by Monte Carlo sampling takes $O(p^{-\lceil d/2 \rceil}/\varepsilon^2)$ samples at physical error rate $p$, code distance $d$ and relative error $\varepsilon$, which becomes intractable at large distances and low error rates, and especially for concatenated codes, whose distance grows as $d^{\ell}$ with the number of levels $\ell$. The fail fast method reduces this cost by sampling the failures of each weight separately, but it only works for unconcatenated codes, and does not model the soft information that the levels of a concatenated code pass to each other. We propose a predictor that takes the stabilizers, the minimum-weight logical operators and, for odd $d$, the logical operators of weight $d + 1$ of a code, and computes, without sampling, the leading monomial $c\,p^{o}$ of the LER when expressed as a polynomial in $p$, at every level of concatenation, in time polynomial in the code parameters and linear in $\ell$ for fixed budgets. We prove that our prediction is exact for any unconcatenated stabilizer code, for every logical observable and arbitrary per-qubit error rates, whenever no budget is exhausted. Furthermore, for concatenated codes, we construct a recursive approach that computes the leading monomial exactly in exponential time, and our predictor approximates this approach. Our predictions match exact enumeration at level 1 on every code we evaluate, and up to three levels for the iceberg code. Using our predictor, we evaluate and compare $37$ code configurations under four noise biases in $48$ core-hours, where Monte Carlo sampling would need more than $10^{12}$ shots at $p = 10^{-3}$ for $113$ of these $148$ cases.

</details>

**Summary.** This work tackles the quantum simulation of $	ext{SU}(N)$ matrix-model dynamics, crucial for understanding black hole physics. The authors develop highly efficient quantum circuits for both near-term (NISQ) and fault-tolerant hardware. By exploiting the mathematical structure of the potential's factorization, they achieve significant reductions in required quantum gates compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides concrete, resource-aware quantum circuit implementations for simulating complex, high-dimensional quantum field theories relevant to quantum gravity and condensed matter models.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the resource cost of compiling the time evolution generated by a complex $	ext{SU}(N)$ matrix-model potential for quantum computation.

**Main result.** The authors propose factorizing the potential into a sum of squared commutator entries, leading to significantly reduced gate counts (both two-qubit and T-gate) compared to standard compilation methods.

**Method.** They derive resource bounds using the Walsh support ($m_{\min}$) and construct specific quantum circuits for both NISQ (using Fourier registers) and fault-tolerant (using reversible arithmetic) hardware.

**Model / system.** The system is the $	ext{SU}(N)$ matrix-model potential $V = -rac{g^2}{4}\sum_{I,J}	ext{Tr}[X_I,X_J]^2$, derived from the BFSS/BMN family, whose dynamics are relevant to black hole physics.

**Key observables.** Two-qubit gate count (NISQ), T-gate count (Fault-Tolerant), and comparison against the theoretical lower bound ($m_{\min}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The scaling depends on the dimension ($d$), matrix size ($N$), and grid size ($Q$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis focuses on compiling the potential term for a single Trotter step, and comparisons are made against specific gate sets and incumbent compilation techniques.

**Figures summary.** The notes mention tables comparing resource requirements across different hardware regimes and circuit types, showing crossover points where the proposed method outperforms incumbents.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical model and the computational challenge, derives theoretical lower bounds, and then presents and verifies two optimized circuit constructions (NISQ and FT) by exploiting the potential's factorization.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The SU$(N)$ matrix-model potential $V=-\tfrac{g^2}{4}\sum_{I,J}Tr[X_I,X_J]^2$, the interaction of the BFSS/BMN family, whose thermal large-$N$ states are dual to black holes, is diagonal in the coordinate basis and is compiled in the literature as a phase polynomial with $O(d^2N^4Q^4)$ rotations per Trotter step. That cost is close to optimal for its gate class: we show that for a generic Trotter step the Walsh support $m_{\min}$ lower-bounds both the rotation count and the two-qubit count of every circuit over $\{CNOT,CZ,CPhase,R_{ZZ},SWAP,X,R_z\}$, ancillas included, and we build a parity network attaining $1.01$--$1.10\,m_{\min}$. Improvement therefore requires a gate outside that class, and the exact factorisation of $V$ into a sum of squared commutator entries supplies one in each era. For NISQ, Hadamard: each squared entry is added into a Fourier register and squared there, $Θ(d^2N^3Q^3)$ two-qubit gates. For fault tolerance, $T$: reversible arithmetic with one phase-gradient injection per squared entry, $Θ(d^2N^3Q^2)$ T gates and no arbitrary-angle rotation. Both are built and verified. With a native $R_{ZZ}$ the NISQ circuit uses fewer two-qubit gates than every parity network from $Q=6$ at SU(2) and $Q=2$ at SU(5); the oracle beats a precision-matched Hamming-weight-phasing incumbent at every point built except the smallest, by up to $11.9\times$ in T count and, at equal width, $25.5\times$ in surface-code spacetime. An ablation with the same arithmetic but no factorisation costs up to $21\times$ more and loses to that incumbent at $15$ of $17$ points, so the factorisation, not the arithmetic, produces the win. Both constructions survive the supersymmetric deformation to mini-BMN with fermions, and complete Trotter evolutions on a statevector simulator reproduce the exact product formula to $2\times10^{-12}$.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents novel symmetry- and AI-assisted methods to discover highly efficient 'magic-state factories' necessary for fault-tolerant quantum computing. By systematically searching the parameter space, the authors found hundreds of new protocols, achieving record low overhead exponents ($\gamma$) for generating essential non-Clifford quantum states. This effort establishes an open-source resource for the quantum community.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work directly tackles fundamental resource limitations in quantum computation, providing concrete, optimized protocols that are crucial for scaling up fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is the resource cost associated with magic-state distillation in fault-tolerant quantum computing, specifically finding protocols for high-distance magic states ($d \ge 3$) at moderate input counts.

**Main result.** The authors discovered 699 factory classes, including 564 new ones, and reported record-setting protocols, such as a pure-T factory achieving $\gamma = 0.998$, which is the smallest known with $\gamma < 1$.

**Method.** They developed symmetry- and AI-assisted search methods, using a unified binary-matrix formulation, where group symmetry and language-model agents guide the search for compatible output gates.

**Model / system.** The context is fault-tolerant quantum computation, focusing on distilling non-Clifford magic states (like T, CS, CCZ) using postselected diagonal CSS protocols. The factories are mathematically represented by binary matrices.

**Key observables.** The overhead exponent ($\gamma = \log(n/k) / \log d$) is the key figure of merit, alongside the number of factory classes found and the minimum T-count.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The distance ($d$), the number of inputs ($n$), and the number of outputs ($k$) are critical parameters defining the factory structure.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The search is restricted to the third level of the Clifford hierarchy, and the initial choice of group symmetry ansatz is sometimes heuristic, guided by AI agents.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 visualizes the distance-three catalog on the $(n, k)$ plane; other figures show catalogs for higher distances and illustrate specific factory structures as circuits and matrices.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by establishing the difficulty of high-distance searches, introducing the unified mathematical framework, detailing the AI-assisted search methodology, presenting the catalog of discovered factories, and concluding with the construction of an open-source repository.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Magic-state distillation is a major resource cost in fault-tolerant quantum computing. The cost of a magic-state factory depends strongly on its failure rate, which grows with the number of input magic states. Although symmetry-restricted methods have recently made distance two searches tractable, distance three and above have remained elusive at moderate input counts. We develop symmetry- and AI-assisted methods to search this regime. We present a unified binary-matrix formulation encompassing both triorthogonal-code and direct circuit searches. We show that distance at least three is equivalent to nonzero, pairwise distinct syndromes, separating the choice of syndromes from the search for compatible output gates. We restrict the syndrome search using group symmetry and language-model agents, followed by deterministic solving and independent verification. Our searches yield 699 factory classes, including 564 new ones. These include factories for pure-T states and factories with entangled outputs comprising combinations of T, CS, and CCZ magic states. The pure-T factories [[63, 11, 3]] and [[850, 128, 6]] achieve the lowest overhead exponents we know among protocols with at most 100 and 1000 inputs, respectively, with $γ= 1.589$ and $γ= 1.057$. Our [[1715, 287, 6]] factory, with $γ= 0.998$, is the smallest known pure-T factory with $γ< 1$. We also provide a context directory of search briefs and campaign notes with which readers can train their own agents and tailor the search to their requirements. With these results, we begin constructing an active, open-source repository of magic-state distillation protocols for the quantum community, supplemented by our methods and data, for the practical fault-tolerant quantum computing regime.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces ToF-PAX-RIXS, a novel, compact instrument that merges Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) with Resonant Inelastic X-ray Scattering (RIXS). By using Photoelectron Spectrometry (PAX) for RIXS analysis, the instrument can measure both single-particle electronic structure and collective excitations on the same sample. This capability is crucial for understanding the complex physics of strongly correlated materials like high-Tc superconductors.

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to combine two powerful, yet technically disparate, spectroscopic techniques (ARPES and RIXS) into one compact platform is highly valuable for condensed matter theorists studying correlated electron systems, as it provides simultaneous access to single-particle and collective excitation spectra.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The need for complementary experimental probes to achieve a comprehensive microscopic description of quantum materials, which exhibit complex electronic behavior arising from interactions between electrons and collective excitations.

**Main result.** The development and demonstration of ToF-PAX-RIXS, a compact instrument capable of correlating single-particle electronic structure (ARPES) and collective excitations (RIXS) on the same sample platform.

**Method.** The instrument combines Time-of-Flight ARPES with RIXS analyzed via Photoelectron Spectrometry (PAX), allowing sequential measurements on the same sample under identical conditions.

**Model / system.** The platform is designed for studying quantum materials, specifically demonstrated on Ca-doped YBa2Cu3O6.45, which are strongly correlated cuprate superconductors. The technique measures photoemission intensity and scattered X-ray photon spectral information.

**Key observables.** Photoemission intensity $I(E_{kin}, k_x, k_y)$ (ARPES) and electron energy/position from photoelectrons generated by absorbed soft X-rays (RIXS).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Energy resolution better than 120 meV; momentum transfer ($\mathbf{Q}$) accessible via photoelectron position.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The measurement relies on the ability to analyze photoelectrons generated from absorbed soft X-rays (PAX) to reconstruct the RIXS spectrum, circumventing the need for large, conventional RIXS spectrometers.

**Figures summary.** Figures detail the mechanical design, CAD overview, and schematic configurations for both ARPES and RIXS measurement modes on the instrument.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the scientific need for combined ARPES and RIXS measurements, details the technical solution using the ToF-PAX-RIXS instrument, benchmarks its performance using $	ext{CaCuO}_2$, and finally demonstrates the combined capability on a cuprate superconductor.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present ToF-PAX-RIXS, a compact instrument that combines time-of-flight momentum-microscopy angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) with resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS). The latter is based on photoelectron spectrometry for analysis of X-rays (PAX). The two techniques are implemented with a single multimode electron-optical column, allowing measurements to be performed sequentially on the same sample under identical experimental conditions. In ARPES mode, the instrument records the photoemission intensity as a function of kinetic energy and two in-plane momentum components. In PAX-RIXS mode, scattered soft X-ray photons are absorbed in a thin metallic converter, and the generated photoelectrons are analyzed in energy and position of emission on the converter. The electron kinetic energy retains the spectral information of the scattered photons, while the position is related to the scattering angle and therefore to the momentum transfer, enabling simultaneous access to a finite momentum-transfer interval. We describe the mechanical design, converter assembly, scattering geometry, and multimode electron optics of the instrument. Its PAX-RIXS performance is benchmarked at the Cu $L_3$ edge using CaCuO$_2$, with Au, Ag, and Pt converters. The measured spectra reproduce the principal features obtained with a conventional grating RIXS spectrometer, and deconvolution yields an effective reconstructed energy resolution better than $120$~meV under the present conditions. Finally, combined ARPES and PAX-RIXS measurements on the same Ca-doped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.45}$ sample demonstrate the capability of the instrument to correlate electronic structure and collective excitations within a common compact platform.

</details>

(b) Here, (i, j) represents all possible combinations from the set {1, 2, 3}, resulting in 6 distinct topologies. (c) Here, (i, j, k) represents all possible permutations from the set {1, 2, 3}, resulting in 6 topologies. (d) Here, i ∈{1, 2, 3}, with j and k being distinct from i and each other, resulting in 3 topologies.</sub>

</details>

**Summary.** This work defines and proves the existence of 'topology-independent quantum advantage' in communication networks. It shows that quantum protocols can outperform all classical protocols even when the classical resource distribution or network topology is unknown. The findings provide a robust theoretical tool for certifying quantum advantages in communication systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of topology-independent advantage provides a robust measure of quantum advantage that is independent of the physical layout of the communication network, which is highly relevant for designing practical quantum communication protocols.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper introduces and rigorously investigates the concept of 'topology-independent quantum advantage' in quantum communication networks.

**Main result.** It establishes that quantum protocols can outperform all classical protocols subject to the same total communication constraint, regardless of the specific communication topology used.

**Method.** The authors characterize the classical correlation polytope by considering the convex hull of correlations achievable across all possible admissible communication topologies (represented by DAGs).

**Model / system.** The model involves $N$ sender parties and one receiver in a communication network. The advantage is tested by comparing quantum achievable rates against the maximum rate achievable by any classical strategy under a total communication resource constraint.

**Key observables.** The success rate of the protocol (e.g., $I_{quantum}$ vs $I_{classical}$), and specific information quantities like $I_5$ and $I_{12}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The total communication resource constraint ($d$), the number of parties ($N$), and the specific input/output alphabet sizes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The classical protocol is free to distribute the total communication resource among parties arbitrarily, and the analysis focuses on the total communication constraint rather than a fixed topology.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate various communication topologies (DAGs) used to characterize the classical correlation polytope, and the analysis uses tables to list facet inequalities.

**Paper structure.** The paper first demonstrates the concept in a simple three-party equality task, then develops a general framework using weighted DAGs to characterize the classical polytope, and finally extends the analysis to four-party networks.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum communication can outperform classical communication in a variety of information-processing tasks, but such advantages are typically established for a fixed communication network. Here we introduce topology-independent quantum advantage, in which a quantum protocol outperforms every classical protocol subject to the same communication constraint, irrespective of how the classical communication resource is distributed among the parties or which communication topology is employed, even when the parties may share unlimited classical randomness. We first demonstrate this phenomenon through a simple three-party equality task: two senders receive ternary classical inputs, while an input-free receiver determines whether the inputs are equal. We then formulate a general framework for topology-independent communication and completely characterize the corresponding classical correlation polytope in the minimal three-party scenario. Its facet inequalities reveal several instances of topology-independent quantum advantage. Remarkably, one of these inequalities enables the semi-device-independent certification of a nonunitary quantum channel, while another certifies a sequential quantum network topology without any prior assumption about the network configuration. Finally, we extend the framework to four-party networks, characterize the relevant classical communication structures, and identify a communication task exhibiting quantum advantages against all admissible classical topologies. Our results establish topology independence as a genuine and robust form of quantum advantage in communication networks.

</details>

**Authors:** Dax Enshan Koh, Triscia Mundo, Iosif Sakos, Antonios Varvitsiotis  
**Type:** theory · **Category:** quantum information and computing · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.05128v1>

**Summary.** This paper proves that training Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) is computationally hard, showing that even finding a local minimum of the objective function is strongly NP-hard. The authors achieve this by reducing the problem from the known hard Stable Set problem to the minimization of a trigonometric polynomial, which is then mapped directly onto a VQA training objective. This establishes a fundamental worst-case computational barrier for variational quantum optimization.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a fundamental theoretical barrier, suggesting that even local optimization in VQAs is computationally intractable in the worst case, which is crucial for understanding the limits of near-term quantum computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the computational hardness of training Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs), specifically focusing on the difficulty of finding local minima of the training objective function.

**Main result.** It proves that finding a local minimum of a VQA training objective, or even approximating a point near it, is strongly NP-hard in the worst case.

**Method.** The proof uses a polynomial-time reduction from the Stable Set problem, transforming the hard combinatorial optimization problem into the minimization of a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial, which is then mapped to the VQA objective function.

**Model / system.** The model is the VQA, which trains parameterized quantum circuits by minimizing an objective function $F(	heta) = \langle 0|U(	heta)^\dagger H U(	heta)|0angle$. The hardness is shown even for simple circuits using single-qubit rotations and commuting observables.

**Key observables.** The training objective function $F(	heta)$, the location of local minimizers $	heta^*$, and the $\ell_p$-distance to these minimizers.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The circuit parameters $	heta \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the distance metric $\ell_p$ ($p \ge 1$), and the size of the graph $G$ used in the reduction.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The hardness result is established for the worst-case scenario, and the proof relies on a dichotomy related to the stable set size $\alpha(G)$ versus a parameter $k$.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the separation of possible local minimizers in the parameter space for the hard trigonometric polynomial instance, and Figure 2 shows the mapping between local minimizers under the trigonometric substitution $T(	heta)$.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the computational barrier by first reducing the Stable Set problem to minimizing a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial, and then constructing an explicit quantum circuit whose VQA training objective reproduces this hard instance.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) generally rely on classical optimization to train parameterized quantum circuits. This training seeks to minimize an objective function, and its efficiency is central to the practical success of these algorithms. However, globally minimizing such training objectives over the circuit parameters is known to be $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, limiting the prospect of general guarantees for efficient training. In this Letter, we prove that even the weaker task of finding a local minimum of such VQA training objectives is strongly $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, including when the objective admits efficient classical evaluation. Moreover, we show that this hardness persists even for the task of finding a parameter vector within $\ell_p$-distance strictly less than $π/2$ of some local minimizer, for every $p\geq 1$. Our central technical result is that approximating a local minimizer of a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial is strongly $\mathsf{NP}$-hard. By explicitly constructing quantum circuits whose training objectives reproduce these hard instances, we obtain a polynomial-time reduction to VQA training. Our results establish a fundamental computational barrier to variational quantum training: even reaching the vicinity of a local minimum remains hard in the worst case.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a universal, entanglement-assisted protocol to boost the worst-case fidelity of quantum channels when multiple noisy channels are available. By constructing a specific superinstrument, the authors demonstrate that the output channel can surpass the fidelity of any individual input channel. This establishes a powerful theoretical tool for quantum communication resource enhancement.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental theoretical tools for understanding how shared quantum resources (like entanglement) can overcome inherent noise limitations in communication protocols, which is central to quantum networking.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of finding a universal method to improve the worst-case fidelity of quantum communication channels when multiple, potentially non-identical channels are used.

**Main result.** It proves that an entanglement-assisted encoding and decoding strategy can universally enhance the worst-case fidelity of quantum channels beyond the fidelity of any single given channel.

**Method.** The authors employ resource theory concepts, constructing an entanglement-assisted superinstrument ($\Theta$) acting on the tensor product of the input channels to achieve the enhancement.

**Model / system.** The system involves quantum communication using $n$ nonidentical quantum channels $\{N_i\}$. The analysis is framed using superchannels and resource theories, particularly focusing on fidelity measures.

**Key observables.** Worst-case fidelity ($F(N)$) and entanglement fidelity ($	ext{Fe}(	ext{N})$) are the primary observables used to quantify channel quality.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of channels ($n$), the initial entanglement fidelities of the channels, and the critical fidelity threshold ($F_c$) are important parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The protocol requires the input channels to satisfy mild assumptions on their initial entanglement fidelities, and the analysis often relies on the ability to perform channel twirling.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the physical decomposition of superchannels and superinstruments, and show the general task of achieving universal channel fidelity improvement.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the problem by defining the goal of universal fidelity improvement, constructs the entanglement-assisted protocol, proves its optimality for specific channels (like depolarizing ones), and then generalizes the findings to classical channels and general resource theories.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Communication using quantum channels generally requires encoding and decoding on many identical uses of a quantum channel. In practical settings, decoherence may severely limit our ability to do so, potentially rendering each channel use nonidentical. Given $n$ nonidentical channels, we present an entanglement-assisted encoding and decoding strategy that yields a channel with higher worst-case fidelity than all of the $n$ given channels. The strategy is universal, in the sense that the improvement holds regardless of what channels are given, as long as they satisfy mild assumptions on their initial entanglement fidelities. Our protocol is optimal when the given channels are depolarizing channels, and is essentially the unique one that is universal. This idea can also be extended to classical channels, where shared randomness between the sender and the receiver allows universal enhancement of the probability of correct transmission. We then consider general quantum resource theories, providing a necessary condition and a sufficient condition for the possibility of such universal improvement of quantum resources.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a deep mathematical correspondence between the zeta functions describing quantum walks on finite paths and continuum spectral determinants. By analyzing the factorization of the discrete zeta function in various limits, the authors show that the discrete structure acts as a 'pre-geometric skeleton' whose continuum limit is governed by the massive Dirac operator. This links quantum walk dynamics to fundamental results in spectral geometry.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between discrete spectral identities (quantum walks) and continuous spectral theory (Dirac operators) via zeta regularization is a powerful tool for understanding spectral properties in quantum systems, linking lattice physics to continuum field theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the 'Walk/Zeta correspondence' by establishing a relationship between the zeta functions of quantum walks on finite path graphs and continuum trace formulas.

**Main result.** The discrete zeta function factorizes into components indexed by the infinite dihedral group, and in the continuum limit, this product matches the Gelfand–Yaglom determinant of a massive Dirac operator.

**Method.** The authors use a generalized reflection principle and a local Konno–Sato correspondence to derive exact discrete trace formulas, which are then analyzed in various scaling limits.

**Model / system.** The model is a quantum walk (Szegedy walk) and a classical random walk on a finite path graph ($P_N$) with reflecting boundaries and arbitrary spatial asymmetry. The analysis compares these discrete systems to their infinite-line counterparts.

**Key observables.** Zeta functions ($\det(I - uP(N))^{-1}$), the boundary factor, and the local factors indexed by the dihedral group.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Asymmetry ($p 
eq q$), the size of the graph ($N$), and scaling parameters ($s, M$) used in the continuum limit.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the existence of the generalized reflection principle and the local Konno–Sato correspondence to establish the factorization.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the discrete factorization of the zeta function, then analyzing the convergence of this factorization in the thermodynamic, diffusive, and ballistic limits, culminating in the identification of the continuum limit with the massive Dirac operator determinant.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We establish a local Konno-Sato correspondence for reflected random and Szegedy walks on a finite path graph. A generalized reflection principle, using explicit involutions rather than point reflections in the asymmetric case, yields exact zeta factorizations into a boundary factor and local factors indexed by the infinite dihedral group. After symmetrization, the classical and quantum local factors correspond for each group element. The identity contribution determines the normalized thermodynamic limits. In the symmetric case, diffusive and ballistic scalings recover the Gaussian Poisson summation formula and the Dirac comb identity, respectively. Under a double scaling of the asymmetry and spectral parameter, the quantum factorization yields a massive Dirac-type limit: nonidentity even words produce the periodic-orbit factor, the identity produces the free-field factor, and odd words together with the boundary produce a finite boundary correction.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously measures the computational cost of running a Variational Quantum Classifier for sentiment analysis, comparing it to classical methods. The key finding is that the VQC training is vastly slower than the classical baseline without providing a reliable, statistically significant accuracy improvement. The work serves as a cautionary feasibility study on the current resource overhead of QNLP simulations.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on NLP, the detailed analysis of resource scaling (time vs. qubits/depth) and the explicit comparison of simulation overhead against classical computation is highly relevant to understanding the resource requirements for any quantum algorithm implementation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper assesses the practical computational cost (energy and compute) associated with running near-term Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) experiments on classical simulators.

**Main result.** The Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) training is found to be significantly slower (thousands of times) than its matched classical baseline, and this increased cost is not offset by a reliable, statistically significant accuracy advantage.

**Method.** The authors measured wall-clock time and estimated energy/CO2 for training a VQC on SST-2 sentiment classification across a grid of 27 configurations, comparing results against classical logistic regression baselines.

**Model / system.** The model is a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) implemented using PennyLane's state-vector simulator. It processes text features (via TF-IDF/PCA) encoded into qubits, followed by a parameterized quantum circuit structure.

**Key observables.** Wall-clock time, Time ratio (VQC time / classical time), Accuracy ($\Delta$), and CodeCarbon estimated energy/CO2 emissions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Qubit counts (4, 6, 8), Circuit depths (1-3 layers), Training set sizes ($N=200, 500, 1000$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The study is limited to a single dataset, representation, ansatz, simulator, and CPU environment, making it a feasibility measurement rather than a general verdict on QNLP.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare VQC validation accuracy vs. training set size, and show the training loss over epochs, illustrating the performance gap between VQC and classical methods.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the need to measure simulator cost in QNLP, details the experimental setup (VQC vs. classical baselines on SST-2), presents the quantitative results on cost scaling and accuracy comparison, and concludes with limitations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Near-term quantum natural language processing (QNLP) experiments often run on classical simulators, so simulator cost is part of the field's practical compute burden, yet accuracy tables do not show it. We measure that cost for a variational quantum classifier (VQC) on binary SST-2 sentiment classification, using PennyLane's state-vector simulator over a controlled grid of 27 configurations: three balanced training-set sizes (N = 200, 500, 1000), three qubit counts (4, 6, 8), and three circuit depths. Each VQC is compared with logistic regression on the same PCA-reduced input; full TF-IDF logistic regression gives an uncompressed reference. The VQC beats its matched baseline in 6 of 27 single-seed comparisons. After reruns at two further seeds, only 1 of these 6 keeps a positive mean advantage larger than its paired seed-to-seed variability, and paired tests on the fixed validation set do not establish it. VQC training is 886-21,127 times slower in measured wall-clock time than the matched classical fit (median 3,158 times); going from 4 to 8 qubits roughly doubles simulator time, and within the tested range per-step cost is well approximated by a linear function of the parameter count. CodeCarbon energy and CO2 estimates are secondary: they imply an almost constant power of about 41 W, so they add little beyond runtime, and we do not build an energy ratio from them. The study is narrow (one dataset, representation, ansatz, simulator, and CPU environment) and is a reproducible feasibility measurement, not a general verdict on QNLP.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates how quantum circuits lose access to high-level synthesis optimizations when their representation changes across different compilers or formats. The authors demonstrate that merely ensuring the computation remains mathematically equivalent is insufficient, as this loss can lead to significantly suboptimal gate counts. They introduce 'Verified,' a novel mechanism that tracks and restores these lost synthesis choices, improving compiler robustness.

**Why it may be interesting.** It highlights a critical, practical gap in quantum software stacks: the gap between mathematical equivalence and compiler optimization potential, which is vital for designing efficient quantum algorithms.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Quantum compilers can lose the ability to apply high-level synthesis optimizations when quantum circuits undergo representation changes (like serialization or format conversion).

**Main result.** Functional equivalence is insufficient; the loss of synthesis availability can significantly increase circuit costs, and a new 'Verified' mechanism is proposed to restore these lost synthesis choices.

**Method.** The authors conducted controlled experiments and repository analyses across major quantum SDKs (Qiskit, TKET, Cirq) by simulating various representation change routes.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on abstract quantum circuits and the compilation process itself, using high-level operations like QFT and MCX gates as test cases.

**Key observables.** Synthesis availability, two-qubit gate count, circuit depth, and the success rate of operation record reconstruction.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The specific quantum compilers (Qiskit, TKET, Cirq) and the type of representation change (OpenQASM 3 round trip, QPY serialization, etc.).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that preserving functional equivalence is not enough; the compiler must also preserve the *potential* for high-level synthesis.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate how direct OpenQASM 3 round trips lose synthesis availability, while the proposed 'Verified' mechanism successfully restores it, often showing a reduction in gate count compared to unverified routes.

**Paper structure.** The paper identifies the problem of synthesis loss during representation changes, analyzes this loss across multiple compiler toolchains and routes, quantifies the resulting circuit cost increases, and finally introduces and validates the 'Verified' recovery mechanism.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum compilers synthesize high-level operations, such as the quantum Fourier transform and multi-controlled X gates, into gate-level circuits. Across compilation stages, a circuit may be serialized, exchanged as OpenQASM, converted between compilers, or lowered to gates. These representation changes can preserve computation while removing the high-level operation itself, leaving the receiving compiler unable to apply a requested synthesis method. We call this loss synthesis availability. We study synthesis availability in Qiskit, TKET, and Cirq through controlled experiments, repository analysis, circuits captured from project tests, and a Munich Quantum Toolkit pipeline. Synthesis availability survives serialization when deserialization restores the high-level operation and survives compiler conversion only when the receiving compiler supports that operation. It does not survive the evaluated OpenQASM routes. After a direct OpenQASM 3 round trip, requested synthesis has no effect in all 360 delivered conditions even though compilation succeeds. In the MQT pipeline, OpenQASM 2 interchange increases the two-qubit gate count by 37.2 percent for an eight-qubit Grover circuit. We also introduce Verified, which records high-level operations before a representation change and reconstructs them only when a check confirms that the record still matches the delivered circuit. Verified restores requested synthesis in all 830 recovery runs, with median verification times from 2.0 to 638 ms per operation family. The check rejects every stale record but also some valid records. These results show that preserving functional equivalence alone is insufficient when later synthesis choices depend on retained high-level structure.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously classifies when the Clifford hierarchy of quantum gates, $C_k(n)$, belongs to the semi-Clifford or generalized semi-Clifford gate sets. Using advanced group theory and symplectic geometry, the authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions based on the hierarchy level $k$ and qubit number $n$. The work provides deep structural insights into the mathematical boundaries of quantum gate sets.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous classification of gate sets within the Clifford hierarchy is fundamental for understanding the computational power and limitations of quantum computation models, which is highly relevant to quantum information theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the mathematical conditions under which the Clifford hierarchy of quantum gates, $C_k(n)$, is contained within the sets of semi-Clifford ($	ext{SC}(n)$) or generalized semi-Clifford ($	ext{GSC}(n)$) gates.

**Main result.** It establishes precise conditions for $	ext{SC}(n)$ membership (e.g., $k\le2$, $n\le2$, or $k=3, n\le6$) and provides structural characterizations and counterexamples showing when $C_k(n)$ fails to be $	ext{GSC}(n)$ for large $k$ and $n$.

**Method.** The analysis employs group theory, symplectic structures over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and conductor descent arguments to constrain the structure of the unitary gates.

**Model / system.** The model is the Clifford hierarchy, $C_k(n)$, which describes a sequence of increasingly complex sets of quantum gates acting on $n$ qubits, related to the Pauli group $P(n)$.

**Key observables.** Membership of the gate set $C_k(n)$ in $	ext{SC}(n)$ or $	ext{GSC}(n)$; the conductor ($	ext{cond}(U)$) of a gate $U$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Hierarchy level $k$ and number of qubits $n$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on mapping gates to vectors in $\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}$ and using Lagrangian subspaces to characterize $	ext{GSC}(n)$.

**Figures summary.** Figures provide tabular summaries of the $(k, n)$ conditions for $	ext{SC}(n)$ and $	ext{GSC}(n)$ membership, and illustrate the inductive process using conductor descent.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first characterizing $	ext{SC}(n)$ membership, then tackling the more general $	ext{GSC}(n)$ membership using conductor arguments, and finally constructing explicit counterexamples (like $U_\xi$) to show when the hierarchy escapes the $	ext{GSC}$ group.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study semi-Clifford and generalized semi-Clifford structures in the Clifford hierarchy as a function of hierarchy level $k$ and qubit number $n$. We show that $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is semi-Clifford if and only if $k\le2$, $n\le2$, or $k=3$ and $n\le6$. We also establish that $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is generalized semi-Clifford when $k\le4$ or $n\le3$ and construct counterexamples when $k,n \geq 5$. For $n=4$ and $k\ge5$, we show that every gate defined over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ up to a scalar is generalized semi-Clifford, reduce the general case to a single level, and propose a strategy to prove our conjecture that $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ is generalized semi-Clifford if and only if $k\le4$ or $n\le4$. Lastly, we go beyond this structure by introducing $n_c$-generalized semi-Clifford gates, which we show are exactly the gates of the form $\sum_x|π(x)\rangle\langle x|\otimes V_x$ up to Clifford gates on both sides, where $π$ permutes the computational basis states of $n_c$ control qubits. We conjecture that for $k\ge3$ every gate in $\mathcal{C}_k(n)$ has this form for some $n_c\ge1$ with every $V_x\in\mathcal{C}_{k-3}(n-n_c)$, refining the conjecture of Zeng, Chen, and Chuang.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces WLPA, a novel, efficient framework for optimally allocating scarce quantum-safe resources like QKD across large networks. It moves beyond simple per-link security assessments by recognizing that system security is limited by the weakest link. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, implementable solution that outperforms standard industry heuristics, especially under sophisticated, targeted attack models.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on network engineering, the underlying mathematical structure—optimizing a global minimum subject to local resource constraints—is analogous to finding the weakest point in a quantum computation or communication chain, making the resource allocation theory relevant to quantum network security.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Network operators must allocate scarce, high-security quantum-safe link postures (like QKD) across a distributed system, where overall security is dictated by the single weakest link.

**Main result.** The authors present WLPA, an algorithm that computes the optimal weakest-link posture assignment in polynomial time, providing a rigorous framework superior to simple per-link heuristics when costs or attack models vary.

**Method.** The core method is developing a closed-form, optimal decision framework (WLPA) that solves a constrained resource allocation problem, validated against integer programming models and various network topologies.

**Model / system.** The system is a distributed network modeled as a graph where links ($e \in ED$) require upgrading to specific quantum-safe postures (Level 1, 2, or 3) constrained by a total QKD budget ($B$) and latency limits ($L$).

**Key observables.** System security (minimum link posture), Breach Probability $B(Q)$, and the optimal achievable security level $S^\star(B, L)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** QKD Budget ($B$), Latency Budget ($L$), Link Compliance Cap ($c_e$), and the three discrete Link Posture Levels.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The security derivation relies on a standard hybrid-argument bound, and the framework assumes a specific model for exploit probability schedules ($p(\ell)$) which are model-calibrated.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison of job breach probability between WLPA and heuristic methods under varying QKD budgets, and show the near-linear runtime scaling of the WLPA algorithm.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the weakest-link security principle, introduces WLPA as the optimal allocation algorithm, proves its correctness and complexity, presents a dichotomy showing when heuristics fail, and validates the framework across 19 diverse experimental scenarios.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Network operators migrating distributed systems to post-quantum and quantum-safe cryptography face a resource-management problem: quantum key distribution (QKD) gives the strongest guarantee available but is hardware-scarce and costly, so only a fraction of a deployment's links can receive it. Default practice -- ranking links by traffic or centrality and upgrading the top scorers -- optimizes each link in isolation, while a distributed job's real security is set by whichever active link ends up weakest. We present WLPA (Weakest-Link Posture Assignment), an implementation-ready decision framework and algorithm for allocating scarce quantum-safe postures under hardware, latency, and compliance constraints. WLPA computes the optimal weakest-link posture in closed form and returns an assignment in O(|E| log |E|) time -- 125 ms for a 20,000-link network on a laptop -- with a breach-aware refinement matching an exact integer program under common conditions. Our central contribution is a dichotomy telling operators exactly when existing per-link heuristics already match this optimum and when they systematically fail: under constant upgrade cost and uniform traffic-driven risk the two coincide exactly; once costs vary or an adversary concentrates on weak targets, heuristics leave the weakest link unprotected, unboundedly. We validate WLPA across 19 experiments: four microservice topologies, a real enterprise network (SNAP email-Eu-core), a post-quantum latency benchmark, a Qiskit BB84 simulation and a real-hardware BB84 run on IBM's ibm_marrakesh processor, checks against real production traffic traces, a CVE-calibrated correlated-compromise study, Bayesian uncertainty quantification, and seven baseline methods. A concrete-security reduction grounds the framework as theoretical foundation, not primary contribution.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper provides a unified theoretical framework to understand Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS), proving that the effect requires breaking both parity and time-reversal symmetry. By analyzing various non-equilibrium transport regimes, the authors demonstrate that coherent chiral vibrations are essential for generating measurable spin polarization, providing a crucial diagnostic tool for future spintronic materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses non-equilibrium spin transport in mesoscopic chiral systems, which is highly relevant to understanding spin-orbit coupling effects in molecular electronics and spintronics, bridging concepts from quantum optics and condensed matter theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The fundamental origin of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS)—the spin polarization of electrons by nonmagnetic chiral systems without external magnetic fields—remains theoretically unsettled.

**Main result.** The authors establish a strict selection rule: measurable CISS signals must be time-reversal odd and vanish near equilibrium, proving structural chirality alone is insufficient. They show that coherent chiral vibrations are necessary to generate substantial, handedness-reversing spin polarization.

**Method.** The study evaluates leading theoretical mechanisms across four levels of non-equilibrium transport, ranging from coherent classical driving to fully non-Markovian quantum baths, using advanced Green's function techniques.

**Model / system.** The analysis employs a minimal single-orbital tight-binding Hamiltonian on a helix, later extended to a more realistic p-orbital model to separate orbital and spin chirality. The system is driven by both coherent and incoherent phonon baths.

**Key observables.** Spin polarization ($P_z$), polarization magnitude (up to 10% for coherent drive), and the reversal of polarization with handedness (Inverse-CISS).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The polarization scales with an effective spin-orbit coupling (SOC), allowing comparison between heavy atoms and curved light-atom backbones.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on modeling the system's response to various phonon coupling mechanisms and assumes the validity of the four levels of non-equilibrium transport theory.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates that equilibrium yields zero polarization due to time-reversal symmetry, while a chiral drive breaks this symmetry, generating spin polarization via the conversion of orbital angular momentum to spin via SOC.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the CISS effect by first establishing the necessary symmetry constraints, then modeling the system using minimal and p-orbital Hamiltonians, and finally testing various non-equilibrium transport regimes (coherent vs. incoherent driving) to pinpoint the required physical mechanism.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

For two decades, the origin of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS), the spin polarization of electrons by nonmagnetic chiral systems without magnetic fields, has remained unsettled. Here, we establish a single exact rule defining the fundamental conditions for the effect: in nonmagnetic, time-reversal-invariant conductors, all measurable CISS signals are time-reversal odd and vanish near equilibrium, proving that structural chirality alone is insufficient. By evaluating leading theoretical mechanisms across four levels of nonequilibrium transport, from coherent classical driving to fully non-Markovian quantum baths, we verify this selection rule to machine precision. We show that coherent chiral vibrations generate substantial collinear polarization (up to 10 percent across 0.5-6 THz) that reverses with handedness, whereas incoherent vibrations yield under 1 percent, and non-Markovian bath memory further suppresses the signal. The chiral geometry first makes the electronic motion chiral by accumulating orbital angular momentum; spin-orbit coupling (SOC) then converts that into spin. CISS therefore acts as both a spin polarizer and a spin filter, the latter an order of magnitude weaker. The polarization grows with molecular length and then saturates, matching trends reported for DNA and peptides. Reversing the drive converts decaying spin into a handedness-locked charge-current pulse (inverse-CISS). We find that once the system is driven, the polarization magnitude scales with an effective spin-orbit coupling: making heavy atoms and curved light-atom backbones indistinguishable at equivalent effective SOC. This enables us to chart how geometry, driving field, and length separate those routes.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study demonstrates that applying a DC bias current to a chiral conductor selects the helicity of its phonons. This selection is driven by an asymmetry in electron-phonon damping, which manifests as a nonconservative Berry force. The effect is robust, leading to a measurable net lattice helicity, and is confirmed using advanced quantum transport calculations on tellurium.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a clear, non-equilibrium mechanism for generating macroscopic quantum coherence (phonon helicity) using only a bias current, connecting electronic transport to lattice dynamics in a chiral setting.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how a DC electric current can induce and select a specific helicity for a chiral phonon in a chiral conductor, leading to a net lattice helicity.

**Main result.** The current generates an asymmetry in phonon damping, which is mathematically equivalent to a nonconservative Berry force, leading to a net, non-zero phonon helicity at any finite bias.

**Method.** The analysis uses non-equilibrium Green's functions (NEGF) and rate equation closures to model the phonon kinetics in an open quantum system driven by a bias voltage.

**Model / system.** The model is a chiral conductor, studied theoretically using a helical tight-binding wire and validated quasi-ab initio calculations on elemental tellurium. The system includes electronic Hamiltonian, phonon bath, and electron-phonon coupling.

**Key observables.** Phonon helicity asymmetry ($\Delta\gamma(V)$), net lattice helicity ($H$), and the transition to a self-sustained coherent travelling wave.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Bias voltage ($V$), phonon wavevector ($q$), and the lattice damping rate ($\gamma_{lat}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The phonon kinetics are closed using a rate equation, and the electronic self-energy is calculated using the Migdal approximation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the transition from equilibrium (zero helicity) to bias-driven selection via damping asymmetry, and finally to a coherent travelling mode above a critical bias ($V_c$).

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory by calculating the current-induced damping asymmetry ($\Delta\gamma$), deriving the resulting net helicity ($H$) via rate equations, and confirming the mechanism through both model calculations and quasi-ab initio simulations on tellurium.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The emergence of spin-polarized electrons from nonmagnetic chiral molecules and crystals is called Chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS). A chiral phonon of definite wavevector $q$ can strongly enhance it, but near equilibrium the two helicities $+q$ and $-q$ are equally populated: they are time-reversal partners and their contributions cancel. We show that in a biased chiral conductor the current causes the phonon of one helicity to damp less than the other. The damping asymmetry is odd in the current, odd under $q\rightarrow-q$, invariant under a mirror that reverses the structural handedness, and equal, mode for mode, to the current-induced nonconservative Berry force on the phonon coordinate. Closing the phonon kinetics with a rate equation turns the asymmetry into a net lattice helicity: at any finite bias one helicity is preferentially populated, with no threshold, growing linearly with the current as $V\rightarrow0$; above a threshold that helicity becomes a self-sustained coherent travelling wave. We demonstrate this effect in elemental tellurium, treated as an open quantum system (electronic Hamiltonian, phonon bath, and electron-phonon coupling) within a quasi-ab initio framework. The electronic Hamiltonian is supplied by a vertex-corrected quasiparticle self-consistent $GW$ (QSGW) potential with spin-orbit coupling; nuclear displacements are modeled with a machine-learned interatomic potential, which yields chiral phonon modes at finite $\pm q_z$ on the $Γ$-A line. The perturbation to the electronic Hamiltonian from a nuclear displacement is approximated by a frozen-phonon deformation potential. No optical pump is needed: a bias alone drives the current and selects the phonon helicity; reversing the current reverses the selection.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a scalable quantum processor architecture for silicon spin qubits by integrating on-chip micromagnets with STM-defined phosphorus donor-cluster arrays. The magnets generate controlled magnetic field gradients, solving the frequency crowding issue that limits qubit addressability. This breakthrough enables the potential integration and addressing of over 120 atomic spin qubits using a single microwave antenna.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the physical implementation challenges of scaling solid-state quantum memories, providing a concrete engineering solution for qubit addressing beyond intrinsic material limitations.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary bottleneck for scaling silicon quantum computing using phosphorus donor-cluster arrays is achieving independent addressability for individual spin qubits due to frequency crowding.

**Main result.** Integrating on-chip micromagnets generates magnetic field gradients that overcome the limitations of hyperfine interaction randomness, enabling the addressability of over 120 atomic spin qubits with a single microwave antenna.

**Method.** The authors combine micromagnetic simulations (using Co magnets) with experimental magnetic field measurements (using SNVM/ODMR) to validate a novel quantum processor architecture.

**Model / system.** The platform uses phosphorus donors in silicon patterned by STM-HDL, forming donor-cluster arrays. The system is enhanced by integrating micromagnets to generate controlled magnetic field gradients ($
abla B$) that shift qubit resonant frequencies.

**Key observables.** Resonant frequencies ($f_{	ext{ESR}}$, $f_{	ext{NMR}}$), magnetic field gradients ($
abla B$), and the lateral range over which a required gradient ($\approx 0.45 	ext{ mT/nm}$) is maintained.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The design aims for scalability to over 120 qubits; the required gradient strength is critical for frequency multiplexing.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial analysis assumes the ideal single-domain behavior of the micromagnets, though discrepancies suggest multi-domain formation and polycrystalline structure are present.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the quantum processor architecture integrating magnets and donor arrays, showing simulated and measured magnetic field components ($B_x, B_y, B_z$) validating the magnet design.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the addressability bottleneck using hyperfine randomness, proposes the micromagnet solution, validates the magnet geometry via micromagnetic simulations, and finally confirms the design feasibility through direct magnetic field measurements.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Phosphorus donors in silicon are one of the promising platforms for fault-tolerant quantum computing, owing to their long coherence times and compatibility with complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology. However, a key bottleneck for scaling this platform lies in the independent addressability of individual spin qubits. Here, we present a scalable quantum processor architecture that integrates scanning tunneling microscope (STM)-defined phosphorus donor-cluster arrays with on-chip micromagnets. By generating magnetic field gradients, the micromagnets enable a broader addressable frequency range compared to the addressing scheme based solely on variations in hyperfine (HF) interactions, which arise from the randomness of intra-cluster configurations. Through micromagnetic simulations to optimize micromagnet geometry, we demonstrate that these structures are compatible with customized array designs, facilitating the integration of over 120 atomic spin qubits and enabling frequency multiplexing with a single microwave antenna, which greatly reduces the overhead of fan-out addressing lines. This design is further validated via magnetic measurements, which generally align with our micromagnetic simulations. These results establish a critical foundation for the development of scalable silicon quantum computing with atomic qubits.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study explores controlling quantum dynamics and entanglement in an exciton-bimodal-cavity system by leveraging an exciton-exciton exchange interaction. By deriving effective Hamiltonians for different energy regimes, the authors show how to engineer long-lived quantum correlations and achieve near-complete population transfer. The results provide direct design rules for realizing coherent excitonic operations in nanoscale platforms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it deals with cavity QED, engineered quantum dynamics, and the control of entanglement in solid-state excitonic systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to demonstrate tunable population transfer and entanglement generation in a two-exciton system coupled to a bimodal optical cavity, incorporating an exciton-exciton exchange interaction.

**Main result.** The study establishes a controllable route for engineering long-lived entanglement and coherent excitonic operations by controlling the exchange interaction, cavity detuning, and light-matter coupling.

**Method.** The authors use dressed-state transformations and Löwdin partitioning to derive effective Hamiltonians, solving the dynamics via the Lindblad master equation.

**Model / system.** The system is a two-exciton system coupled to a bimodal optical cavity, modeled using a full Hamiltonian that includes exciton energies, cavity frequencies, coupling strengths, and an exchange interaction term. The analysis is applied to graphene nanoribbon excitons.

**Key observables.** Population transfer, entanglement concurrence, beat period, and excitonic coherent-cycle number.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Exchange interaction strength (J), cavity detuning, and light-matter coupling strength (g). The dynamics are analyzed in small/moderate and large-exchange regimes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the use of the rotating-wave approximation and often focuses on the single-excitation subspace or specific energy regimes for simplification.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the system schematic, show population and entanglement dynamics for varying exchange interactions (small vs. large J), and present engineering maps relating beat period, transfer amplitude, and coherent cycles to control parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by defining the full Hamiltonian and dynamics, then systematically decomposing the problem into effective Hamiltonians for different physical regimes (excitonic, local polaritonic, beat-polaritonic) using advanced mathematical techniques before deriving control rules.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We theoretically demonstrate tunable population transfer and entanglement generation in a two-exciton system coupled to a bimodal optical cavity, including an exciton-exciton exchange interaction. By using dressed-state transformations and Löwdin partitioning, we derive effective Hamiltonians that identify three dynamical time scales: local polaritonic oscillations, long-period dressed-state beats, and direct excitonic exchange. We apply the framework to graphene nanoribbon excitons, using excitonic energies, transition dipoles, and lifetimes obtained from first-principles calculations to parameterize the model. In the small- and moderate-exchange regimes, the dynamics become multiscale, and the beat channel sustains sizable quantum entanglement over long dissipative time windows. In the large-exchange regime, the excitonic Hamiltonian dominates and drives nearly complete population transfer between excitonic states over many coherent cycles. The resulting analytical expressions provide direct design rules connecting the beat period, transfer amplitude, and coherent-cycle number to the exchange interaction, cavity detuning, and light--matter coupling. Our results establish a controllable route for engineering long-lived entanglement and coherent excitonic operations in exciton--bimodal-cavity systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work presents a novel superconducting diode that operates without external magnetic fields by using biharmonic microwave driving. By controlling the relative phase of the drive, the device can dynamically switch between operating as a Cooper-pair diode or a quasiparticle diode. This approach yields high-efficiency, tunable rectification suitable for next-generation low-power cryogenic electronics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The use of microwave driving to engineer quantum interference effects in a superconducting junction to achieve directional transport is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum electronics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is achieving reliable, non-reciprocal (diode-like) electronic transport at sub-Kelvin temperatures, overcoming the limitations of conventional semiconductor diodes in cryogenic regimes.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate a field-free, dynamically reconfigurable superconducting diode using a single junction driven by biharmonic microwave excitation, achieving rectification efficiencies surpassing existing devices.

**Method.** The study combines theoretical derivations based on multi-photon tunneling (Fermi's golden rule) with semiclassical modeling (RSJ model) to predict and interpret experimental measurements.

**Model / system.** The system is a conventional Al/AlOx/Al superconducting tunnel junction (SIS junction). Operation is controlled by applying a biharmonic microwave drive, which allows independent control over both dissipationless Cooper-pair and dissipative quasiparticle tunneling channels.

**Key observables.** Diode efficiency ($\eta_{QP}, \eta_S$), I-V characteristics under varying drive phases ($	heta$), and the identification of zero forward resistance and strongly suppressed reverse conduction.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relative phase ($	heta$) of the microwave drive, the superconducting gap energy ($\Delta$), and the ratio of drive amplitudes ($k=V_2/V_1$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the applicability of the Tien-Gordon model extension and relies on the ability to isolate and control the distinct Cooper-pair and quasiparticle tunneling mechanisms.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the operational concepts (Quasiparticle, Supercurrent, Absolute diode), show I-V curves comparing theoretical models to experimental measurements, and detail AC rectification measurements in both regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the need for cryogenic diodes to developing the theoretical framework using biharmonic driving to break symmetry, calculating the resulting transport channels (QP and Cooper-pair), and finally demonstrating the tunable 'absolute diode' behavior.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Non-reciprocal transport underpins key functionalities in signal processing and logic; however, conventional semiconductor diodes exhibit reduced performance at sub-Kelvin temperatures. As cryogenic electronics continue to scale, there is increasing demand for diode operation compatible with low-temperature and low-dissipation conditions. This need has driven the development of alternatives to p-n junctions that rely on non-reciprocal electron transport mechanisms efficient in the deep-cryogenic regime. Superconducting devices constitute a natural low-loss platform, yet most existing superconducting diodes are restricted to either Cooper-pair or quasiparticle transport, often requiring complex material stacks, asymmetric geometries, or external magnetic fields. No single, geometrically symmetric junction has yet integrated rectification across both transport channels to achieve vanishing resistance under forward bias and strongly suppressed conduction under reverse bias. Here, we demonstrate a dynamically reconfigurable dual-function superconducting diode based on a conventional Al/AlOx/Al tunnel junction. Via microwave biharmonic driving, we exploit multi-tone photon-assisted tunneling to independently control dissipationless and dissipative transport channels within the same device. Varying the microwave drive amplitude induces a transition from a supercurrent diode to an ideal quasiparticle diode, achieving rectification efficiencies exceeding those of conventional Schottky diodes and contemporary superconducting diodes. We further demonstrate AC signal rectification under both current-bias and voltage-bias configurations. Finally, we implement a proof-of-concept "absolute diode" that combines zero forward resistance with strongly suppressed reverse conduction. This tunable approach provides a versatile building block for low-power cryogenic electronic architectures.

</details>
