**Summary.** This theoretical work develops an exact four-sector decomposition for the shift conductivity, a measure of photocurrent, by analyzing the singular field structure of the shift vector on the Brillouin torus. It demonstrates that while global invariants like the Chern number are important, the local winding of charges at band edges dictates the sign and magnitude of the photocurrent. This provides a powerful framework for analyzing topological responses in 2D materials like graphene bilayers.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical decomposition of a physical response function (photocurrent) into geometrically distinct, quantifiable sectors (vortex, Berry, etc.) provides powerful tools for understanding topological responses in condensed matter systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to find an exact decomposition of the shift conductivity, a second-order photocurrent, based on the quantum geometry of Bloch bands.

**Main result.** The shift conductivity is shown to have an exact four-sector decomposition, where the integer charge sector accounts for band-edge peaks, and the sign of the photocurrent is governed by the winding of a single charge rather than the global Chern number.

**Method.** The core method involves inverting the curl relation for the shift vector field on the Brillouin torus using the Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition, splitting the conductivity into contributions from vortices, Berry curvature, and gradients.

**Model / system.** The analysis is applied to two-band models, specifically using a graphene-Haldane bilayer and a time-reversal-symmetric biased AB bilayer Hamiltonian.

**Key observables.** Shift conductivity ($\sigma_{a;bb}(\omega)$), shift vector ($\mathbf{R}$), interband Berry curvature ($\Omega_{cv}$), and quantized point charges ($n_i$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Frequency ($\omega$), Chern number ($\chi_{cv}$), and the warping parameter ($\gamma_3$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to a single pair of bands and one component, and it treats remote bands as virtual states.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the decomposition of $\sigma_{y;yy}(\omega)$ into four sectors, showing that the vortex sector ($\sigma_{vort}$) accounts for the entire band-edge peak, and demonstrate the linear and sign-reversing profile of the band-edge charge with warping.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the mathematical decomposition identity using Hodge theory on the torus, applies this to physical models like graphene bilayers, and then analyzes the specific physical implications of the integer charge sector versus the global topological invariant (Chern number).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Does any integer survive in the shift current, and does the Chern number control its sign? We show that the shift vector is a singular field on the Brillouin torus. Its curl has two sources: the interband Berry curvature and quantised point charges at the zeros of the transition dipole. Inverting this relation gives an exact decomposition of the shift conductivity, valid at every frequency, into one sector linear in the integer charges and three continuous sectors. As a testing ground, we take a graphene-Haldane bilayer: a model that lets us sweep the interband Chern number through five values at fixed gap to isolate its role. We also test the formalism against the time-reversal-symmetric biased AB bilayer. Whenever a charge sits at the band edge, and trigonal warping is present, the integer sector alone accounts for the band-edge peak. The relevant integer is not the Chern number but the winding of that single charge. Its sign, combined with a valley-dependent profile, sets the sign of the photocurrent. In these bilayers, sign reversals across topological transitions follow this winding; the invariant changes with it only when the same gap closing does both. A band-edge charge needs no invariant. It only requires that the two band-edge sublattices not be connected by the nearest-neighbour hopping, and trigonal warping makes it visible.

</details>

**Summary.** This review surveys the use of 3D nanopatterning techniques, specifically FEBID and FIBID, to create complex nanostructures from superconducting and magnetic materials. It details how controlling the geometry—such as introducing chirality or curvature—allows researchers to access and study emergent physical phenomena that are inaccessible in bulk samples. The work highlights the potential of these methods for next-generation quantum device prototyping.

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to engineer geometry at the nanoscale allows for the controlled study of topological and curvature-induced effects in quantum materials, which is highly relevant for understanding emergent quantum phenomena.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of extending quantum materials into the third dimension (3D) to geometrically tune emergent properties beyond those found in bulk materials.

**Main result.** Focused electron and ion beam induced deposition (FEBID/FIBID) are powerful techniques enabling the realization of complex 3D nanostructures for studying emergent magnetic and superconducting phenomena.

**Method.** The review discusses the capabilities and underlying mechanisms of 3D nanopatterning using FEBID and FIBID, which allow for direct writing of functional materials.

**Model / system.** The physical systems studied are superconducting and magnetic materials patterned into complex 3D nanostructures, allowing control over chirality, curvature, and topology.

**Key observables.** Magnetization structures (e.g., domain walls, vortices), persistent currents, and superconducting screening currents.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The study operates in an intermediate regime between the superconducting coherence length ($\xi \sim 5-10 	ext{ nm}$) and the London penetration depth ($\lambda \sim 450-850 	ext{ nm}$); resolution is key, down to the few nanometers.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary limitation noted is the experimental challenge of maintaining fidelity and achieving uniform properties in highly complex, sub-100 nm 3D geometries.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the variety of 3D nanostructure architectures achievable via FEBID/FIBID, including chiral, curved, and topologically non-trivial designs.

**Paper structure.** The review systematically discusses the necessity of 3D patterning, details the capabilities of FEBID/FIBID, and then analyzes the specific emergent effects observed in magnetic (e.g., domain walls) and superconducting (e.g., Meissner currents) nanostructures based on geometry.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The extension of nanoscale quantum materials to the third dimension brings new possibilities to geometrically tune emergent properties, emulating or indeed going beyond the physics of bulk materials, with exciting implications for high-density technological integration. Realising such three-dimensional architectures requires nanofabrication techniques that not only enable complex 3D geometries, but also deliver functional quantum materials with emergent phenomena. Recent advances in focused electron- and ion-beam induced deposition (FEBID and FIBID) have made 3D nanopatterning of functional materials in complex geometries increasingly feasible, paving the way for the experimental realisation of new phenomena and device prototyping. In this review, we discuss the use of FEBID and FIBID 3D nanopatterning of superconducting and magnetic materials. We address the underlying mechanisms, and capabilities of these techniques, focusing on the physical phenomena that become accessible. Considering the resolution of the techniques in the context of the fundamental lengthscales of the materials, we discuss the emergent effects that arise due to three dimensional geometries in magnetic and superconducting nanostructures, and highlight perspectives for future developments of the techniques.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes soliton dynamics in the non-integrable Gardner-Ostrovsky equation, which models wave propagation in dispersive media. Through numerical simulations, the authors demonstrate that soliton interactions are inelastic, causing energy to transfer from smaller solitons to a single, dominant 'soliton-champion.' This highlights a fundamental energy redistribution mechanism in this non-integrable physical model.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical nonlinear PDEs, the concept of energy absorption and the emergence of a dominant structure from complex, interacting localized excitations shares conceptual parallels with energy transfer mechanisms studied in open quantum systems or nonlinear wave phenomena in quantum optics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the formation and complex, inelastic interactions of solitons within the non-integrable Gardner-Ostrovsky (GO) equation.

**Main result.** Soliton interactions are inherently inelastic, leading to a 'soliton-champion' effect where the largest-amplitude soliton absorbs energy from smaller ones. The GO equation models wave dynamics in dispersive media.

**Method.** The research employs numerical methods, including the Petviashvili method, to construct and simulate soliton solutions and their subsequent interactions.

**Model / system.** The system is governed by the Gardner-Ostrovsky equation, a generalization of the Gardner equation incorporating cubic nonlinearity and rotational dispersion, relevant to plasmas and oceanic internal waves.

**Key observables.** Soliton amplitude, velocity, energy transfer, and the existence of stationary bound states (bi-solitons).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dispersion regime requires anomalous (positive) dispersion ($eta > 0$), and the interaction dynamics depend on the nonlinear coefficient ($\delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes small amplitudes for linear properties and that the GO equation is non-integrable, which dictates the inelastic nature of the interactions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dispersion relation, soliton amplitude vs. speed, soliton shapes, and time evolution of pulse amplitudes during head-on collisions and interactions with bi-solitons.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from linear analysis and numerical construction of solitons to detailed simulations of multi-soliton interactions, culminating in the demonstration of the energy-transferring 'soliton-champion' effect.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate soliton formation and interactions in the non-integrable Gardner-Ostrovsky equation (alias the rotation-modified Gardner equation) with anomalous (positive) dispersion. This equation is relevant to the description of wave dynamics in plasmas and other dispersive media. We show that a special class of solitons, characterized by zero total mass and non-monotonic asymptotics, can emerge from pulse-like initial perturbations. Depending on the initial conditions, these solitons may form regular amplitude-ordered trains, irregular nonstationary ensembles of interacting localized structures, or stationary propagating multi-soliton complexes. We further demonstrate that soliton interactions in the Gardner-Ostrovsky equation are inherently inelastic, leading to the emergence of a dominant "soliton-champion" in closed systems. For example, under periodic boundary conditions, only the largest-amplitude soliton ultimately survives, while all smaller solitons are gradually eliminated through successive interactions. Despite their inelastic interactions, Gardner-Ostrovsky solitons exhibit remarkable robustness.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors present a novel, all-microwave technique using magnonic coherent splitting in YIG to image microwave magnetic fields. By measuring the spectral splitting between two magnon modes, they achieve high sensitivity and temporal resolution for mapping magnetic field distributions. This method proves valuable for non-destructive diagnostics of high-frequency circuits and spintronic devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work demonstrates a novel, all-microwave sensing modality for magnetic fields in functional devices, providing a powerful tool for characterizing high-frequency dynamics without relying on optics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to develop a room-temperature, optics-free method for spatiotemporal imaging of microwave magnetic fields, which is crucial for diagnosing high-frequency circuits and studying nonequilibrium spin dynamics.

**Main result.** The technique successfully reconstructs microwave magnetic fields across position and time, demonstrating high sensitivity (58 pT/sqrt(Hz)) and resolving dynamic events like switching and faults in RF amplifiers.

**Method.** The method utilizes magnonic coherent splitting in YIG, where the target magnetic field amplitude is transduced into a measurable spectral splitting via coupling between a pump-induced magnon mode and a Walker mode.

**Model / system.** The physical system is Yttrium iron garnet (YIG) exhibiting ferrimagnetic order. The mechanism relies on the coherent coupling between a pump-induced magnon mode (PIM) and a Walker mode (WM), providing a calibrated relationship between the field and the spectral splitting.

**Key observables.** Spectral splitting magnitude (related to field amplitude $B$), phase ($\phi$), and time-resolved field evolution $B(r, 	au)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Sensitivity of 58 pT/sqrt(Hz); time resolution of 130-ns; operating at room temperature.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes the PIM–WM coupling strength provides a reliable, calibrated link to the magnetic field amplitude $B$.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the field-to-splitting transduction mechanism, calibration curves showing $g(B)$ vs. $B$, and protocols for both spatial and time-resolved imaging.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the theoretical basis of the coherent splitting, presents the experimental setup for spatial and temporal mapping, validates the magnetic selectivity against electric field measurements, and applies the technique to diagnose faults in an RF amplifier.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Spatiotemporal microwave magnetic-field imaging reveals current flow in high-frequency circuits and nonequilibrium spin dynamics, yet probes rarely combine calibrated spectral readout, optics-free operation and transient mapping at room temperature. Here ferrimagnetic order in yttrium iron garnet supports coherent coupling from a pump-induced magnon mode, converting target-field amplitude into a spectral splitting with all-microwave readout. Sampling the calibrated splitting over position and delay reconstructs spatiotemporal imaging of magnetic fields. Continuous-wave measurement reaches a sensitivity of 58 pT/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and recovers phases across various powers. Combined with time-resolved frequency-comb spectroscopy, the method reconstructs transient fields with a 130-ns response time. Coplanar-waveguide imaging validates the magnetic selectivity of the mode-splitting readout, where measured maps agree with simulated magnetic-field distribution. In a microwave amplifier, our reconstruction resolves nonuniform switching dynamics and detects downstream field suppression from an open-contact fault. Magnonic coherent splitting provides a scalable route for optics-free imaging of spatiotemporal field evolution in functional devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work characterizes surface-pinned, topologically charged defects in light scattering from plasmonic nanostructures. The defects are purely topological, arising from boundary conditions, and their existence is confirmed through charge-conserving bifurcations. The study highlights that these defects are robust features of the electromagnetic field structure, independent of surface energy models.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous topological classification of field structures in plasmonics provides a powerful, geometry-independent diagnostic tool for understanding light-matter interactions at interfaces, which has implications for designing advanced optical components.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the existence and properties of surface-pinned, topologically charged, nonsingular defects (SDs) that arise in light scattering from plasmonic objects.

**Main result.** These defects are purely topological, dictated by Maxwell boundary conditions, and are found in the electric and Poynting vector fields for H(z) polarization, demonstrating topological charge conservation during field bifurcations.

**Method.** The analysis uses exact solutions for light scattering (e.g., for a cylinder) and defines the topological charge via the winding number calculated from one-sided traces of the field components at the material interface.

**Model / system.** The study models light scattering from a plasmonic object, specifically analyzed in (quasi) 2D at optical frequencies, using the framework of Maxwell's equations.

**Key observables.** The local and global winding numbers ($w_E, w_S$), the field patterns in the E and Poynting vector fields, and the evolution of defect domains in parameter space.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Optical frequencies, dissipation ($\varepsilon''$), and the material permittivity ($\varepsilon'$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is simplified to 2D scattering by an infinite cylinder, and the topological charge is defined by regularizing the sharp boundary interface.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematic field lines near an SD, charge-conserving annihilation processes involving bulk saddles and SDs, and maps showing domains of different SD winding numbers in the parameter space.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical basis for SDs from Maxwell's equations, demonstrates their existence and properties using exact solutions (e.g., for a cylinder), analyzes the topological charge conservation through bifurcations, and examines the effect of dissipation on these structures.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We discuss surface-pinned, topologically charged, nonsingular defects (SD) in light scattering by a plasmonic object. They follow from exact Maxwell boundary conditions and are purely topological---unaffected by surface forces. At optical frequencies, in (quasi) 2D, they appear in the electric and Poynting vector fields for $H^{(z)}$ polarization, not for $E^{(z)}$. Exact solutions for a circular cylinder reveal topological charge-conserving bifurcations involving SDs with bulk singularities or SDs alone, and contraction of defect regions under loss.

</details>

**Summary.** This work pioneers the use of cryogenic, polarization-sensitive terahertz nanoscopy to measure the Bulk Photovoltaic Effect (BPVE) in bilayer graphene. By employing near-field techniques, the authors successfully disentangle the intrinsic quantum-geometric photovoltaic signal from background photothermoelectric noise. This provides an optical lens into the fundamental interplay between band structure and quantum geometry in advanced 2D materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to optically probe quantum geometric effects like the BPVE at the nanoscale using THz spectroscopy provides a powerful, non-equilibrium tool for characterizing band structure and symmetry in 2D materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a technique to spatially and spectroscopically separate the intrinsic Bulk Photovoltaic Effect (BPVE) from confounding contact- and interface-induced photothermoelectric signals.

**Main result.** The study successfully demonstrated the nanoscale mapping of the BPVE in bilayer graphene, confirming its dependence on quantum geometry and revealing signatures of electronic structure details like trigonal warping.

**Method.** The authors employed cryogenic, polarization-sensitive terahertz microscopy, specifically utilizing near-field scanning optical microscopy (s-SNOM) to achieve deep-subwavelength spatial resolution.

**Model / system.** The physical system is dual-gated AB bilayer graphene, whose electronic properties are governed by quantum geometry, linking the BPVE to nonlinear light-matter interactions.

**Key observables.** Spatially resolved local photovoltage amplitude ($V_{ph}$), polarization-dependent photovoltage ($\propto \cos(2	heta - \phi)$), and the evolution of BPVE with carrier density ($n$) and displacement field ($D$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Terahertz photon energy ($\hbar\omega \approx 10.5 	ext{ meV}$), cryogenic temperature ($12 	ext{ K}$), and the characteristic twofold angular symmetry.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on separating the intrinsic bulk response from extrinsic contributions, which is achieved by modeling the polarization dependence using an extraction anisotropy function.

**Figures summary.** Figures show the device architecture and far-field THz measurements, followed by near-field maps showing photovoltage vs. (n, D), and polarization dependence plots illustrating the separation of PTE, detected BPVE, and reconstructed intrinsic BPVE.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the need for advanced measurement techniques (far-field limitations) to implementing near-field s-SNOM measurements. It then details the rigorous polarization-resolved analysis to mathematically decompose the total signal into its intrinsic BPVE, PTE, and geometric coupling components.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE) provides a direct link between quantum geometry and nonlinear light-matter interactions, yet conventional far-field measurements cannot disentangle BPVE from contact- and interface-induced photothermoelectric signals. Here we develop cryogenic, polarization-sensitive terahertz microscopy with deep-subwavelength resolution and apply it to dual-gated AB bilayer graphene. Near resonance between the band gap and terahertz photon energy, we observe enhanced optical conductivity and spatially resolved BPVE. Polarization-dependent measurements reveal a characteristic twofold angular symmetry and a distinct shift-vector direction, both governed by crystalline symmetries and quantum geometry. The evolution of BPVE with carrier density and temperature provides a sensitive probe of the fine electronic structure of bilayer graphene, revealing signatures of trigonal warping and electron-hole asymmetry. Agreement with theory demonstrates that the terahertz nanoscopy of BPVE established here offers an optical lens into the interplay between band and quantum geometry in quantum materials.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper generalizes the Wen-Zee coupling, which relates electric charge to curvature in Quantum Hall systems, to the context of 2+1-dimensional gravity. It calculates how this coupling contributes to the black hole's Wald entropy, finding a non-trivial horizon boost charge. The work successfully bridges concepts from topological quantum field theory and gravitational thermodynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection drawn between topological invariants from condensed matter (Quantum Hall effect) and fundamental gravitational thermodynamics (Black Hole Entropy) is highly relevant for theoretical physicists studying emergent quantum field theories in curved spacetime.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the contribution of a mixed gauge-curvature coupling, analogous to the Wen-Zee term, to the Wald entropy in 2+1-dimensional gravity.

**Main result.** The coupling contributes a horizon boost charge to the Wald entropy, which can be non-zero even if the mixed term vanishes on shell, connecting quantum Hall physics to gravitational thermodynamics.

**Method.** The authors use the Wald construction and Noether charge formalism to calculate the entropy contribution arising from a generalized, Lorentz-covariant gauge-curvature coupling term.

**Model / system.** The study models 2+1-dimensional gravity, incorporating topological Chern-Simons theories, quantum Hall fluid descriptions (via the Wen-Zee term), and analyzing backgrounds like AdS-Lorentz black holes.

**Key observables.** Wald entropy contribution, horizon Lorentz-boost charge, Hall conductance ($
u$), and related topological quantities.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The coupling constant $eta$, the curvature $R$, and the gauge field $A_a$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the existence of a Lorentz-covariant generalization of the Wen-Zee term and utilizes the framework of Chern-Simons gravity based on the Maxwell algebra.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory by first establishing the necessary couplings (using both Euler current and extended Maxwell algebra approaches) and then applying the Wald formalism to calculate the resulting entropy contribution on specific black hole and cosmological backgrounds.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Wen-Zee term is a mixed gauge-curvature coupling in the topological Chern-Simons description of a quantum Hall fluid, encoding the electric charge bound to spatial curvature. We investigate a Lorentz-covariant generalisation of this coupling, expanding its scope to black-hole spacetimes and determine its contribution to horizon entropy. Such a coupling arises naturally in three-dimensional Chern-Simons gravity based on the Maxwell algebra. We show that its Wald entropy contribution is a horizon boost charge, given by a loop integral of the additional gauge field projected along the tangent to the bifurcation circle. This contribution can be nonzero even when the mixed term vanishes on shell. We show that the integral admits an Abelian holonomy interpretation when the projection direction is covariantly constant. We evaluate the charge on a flat cosmological solution and, using smooth horizon fields and a specified thermal ensemble, on an AdS-Lorentz black hole. These results connect the geometric response familiar from quantum Hall physics to gravitational horizon thermodynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces MoiréMLIP, a machine-learned potential trained specifically on moiré materials to overcome the computational barriers of simulating large, twisted superstructures. By fine-tuning and compressing this model, the authors created a highly accurate potential capable of simulating systems up to one million atoms. This enables predictive simulations of complex phenomena, such as hierarchical polarization networks, in emergent moiré systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The development of highly accurate, scalable MLIPs for moiré systems provides a powerful tool for simulating emergent electronic and structural phenomena in 2D materials, which is crucial for understanding correlated electron physics in these systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Direct ab initio modeling of large, complex moiré superstructures is computationally prohibitive due to the high dimensionality of structural degrees of freedom.

**Main result.** The authors developed MoiréMLIP, a fine-tuned machine-learning potential, which accurately reproduces DFT reconstructions and scales to one million atoms using knowledge distillation.

**Method.** They fine-tuned a universal MLIP on a specialized dataset (Moiré Kaleidoscope) and employed knowledge distillation to create a highly accurate, yet computationally efficient, student model.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on moiré lattices formed by twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) like MoTe2. The model aims to capture complex structural reconstructions arising from moiré supercells.

**Key observables.** Force Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE), interlayer distance differences (e.g., $\Delta d_{	ext{MM}-	ext{MX}}$), and the emergent polarization network.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Twist angles (e.g., 7.34$^\circ$, 5.09$^\circ$, 3.48$^\circ$), system size (up to one million atoms), and force error thresholds (e.g., 6--8 meV/Å).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that fine-tuning a universal MLIP on a comprehensive dataset can overcome the limitations of existing potentials when applied to novel moiré geometries.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the workflow of dataset construction, the learning curves showing force RMSE reduction with training data volume, and the comparison of reconstruction profiles across different models.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of moiré materials, introduces the MoiréMLIP methodology via dataset curation and fine-tuning, validates its accuracy against DFT benchmarks, and finally applies the model to predict emergent physical properties like polarization in large-scale systems.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Atomic reconstruction reshapes moiré materials across multiple scales, from local structure and polarization textures to global electronic topology, yet direct \textit{ab initio} modeling becomes prohibitive for large superstructures such as marginal-twist-angle moirés and moiré-of-moirés. We develop MoiréMLIP by fine-tuning a universal atomistic model on the density functional theory labeled Moiré Kaleidoscope dataset, which spans transition metal dichalcogenide compositions, symmetries, stackings, and twist angles. MoiréMLIP reproduces \textit{ab initio} reconstruction with force errors of 6--8\,meV/Å and transfers to smaller twist angles and unseen structures. Knowledge distillation yields MoiréMLIP-mini, which retains this accuracy while extending single-GPU inference to one million atoms. Applied to an alternate-twist MoTe$_2$ trilayer, it reveals a hierarchical polarization network spanning tens of nanometers arising from large moiré-cell distortions sharply localized along the moiré-of-moiré domain walls. These results overcome key accuracy, transferability, and scaling bottlenecks of existing atomistic models and enable predictive simulations across emergent moiré length scales.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports the observation of large and highly gate-tunable second- and third-order nonlinear Hall effects in $	ext{BiSbTeSe}_2$ topological insulators. By utilizing dual-gating, the researchers demonstrated that these nonlinear responses are strongly dependent on the Fermi level position relative to the Dirac point. This establishes a promising experimental platform for developing next-generation electronic devices based on topological properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** While the primary focus is condensed matter transport, the strong dependence of the nonlinear response on topological invariants (like BCD/BPT) provides a rich platform for studying quantum geometric effects in electronic transport, which can inform theoretical models of quantum materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to explore and engineer a strong and highly tunable Nonlinear Hall Effect (NLHE) for use in next-generation electronic devices.

**Main result.** Large, highly gate-tunable second-order and third-order NLHEs were observed in dual-gated $	ext{BiSbTeSe}_2$, with the second-order effect showing higher generation efficiency than previous topological insulator systems and remaining stable up to room temperature.

**Method.** The researchers measured the second-order ($2\omega$) and third-order ($3\omega$) nonlinear Hall voltages by applying an a.c. excitation current and using lock-in amplification, while tuning the Fermi level via dual-gating.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a dual-gated topological insulator, $	ext{BiSbTeSe}_2$, where transport is dominated by topological surface states (TSSs). The measurements are performed by modulating the gate voltages to tune the Fermi level relative to the Dirac point (CNP).

**Key observables.** Second-order nonlinear Hall voltage ($V_{xy}^{2\omega}$), third-order nonlinear Hall voltage ($V_{xy}^{3\omega}$), and the nonlinear Hall generation efficiencies ($\eta^{(2)}$ and $\eta^{(3)}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gate voltage ($V_{tg}, V_{bg}$), temperature (up to 300 K), and the proximity to the Charge Neutrality Point (CNP).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on scaling arguments linking the observed signals to specific physical mechanisms, such as the Berry curvature dipole (BCD) or Berry connection polarizability tensor (BPT).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the gate-dependent mapping of $R_{xx}$ and the nonlinear Hall voltages, confirming tunability near the CNP. Temperature dependence studies show the persistence of the second-order effect up to room temperature.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically measures the nonlinear response at different temperatures and gate biases, analyzes the scaling of the nonlinear coefficients with the longitudinal conductance squared, and discusses the microscopic origins of the observed effects based on theoretical models.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) holds significant promise for next-generation electronic device applications, and it is essential to explore and engineer a strong and highly tunable NLHE. In this work, we report large second-order and third-order NLHEs in dual-gated BiSbTeSe2 devices. Both the second-order and third-order NLHE are highly gate-tunable. The second-order NLHE exhibits a higher generation efficiency than those reported in previous topological insulator systems, and it can be stably observed up to room temperature. Meanwhile, the generation efficiency of the third-order NLHE is comparable to previously reported values. The scaling analysis indicates that the second-order NLHE is consistent with contributions from skew scattering and a term compatible with either the Berry curvature dipole or side jump, whereas the third-order NLHE is consistent with contributions from the Berry connection polarizability tensor and higher-order skew scattering. Our work establishes a promising experimental platform for the development of NLHE-based devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work proposes using Multi-bit Ferroelectric-NAND (FE-NAND) memory as a viable in-storage compute architecture to overcome the bottlenecks of traditional von Neumann computing for massive database searches. By engineering the FE-NAND stack, the authors demonstrate high-density, energy-efficient computation of hyperdimensional similarity metrics. The results show massive speed and energy gains over current state-of-the-art solutions.

**Why it may be interesting.** Not directly relevant

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The growing demand for large-scale database search exposes fundamental limitations in von Neumann architectures due to memory bandwidth and energy constraints.

**Main result.** The proposed FE-NAND in-storage compute architecture achieves nearly 1,000x speedup and over 10,000x energy efficiency improvement for massive database search tasks.

**Method.** The authors demonstrate in-situ multi-level cell (MLC) dot product operations and calculate Hamming similarity using planar Ferroelectric NAND (FE-NAND) strings.

**Model / system.** The platform utilizes engineered FE-NAND strings (with $	ext{Al}_2	ext{O}_3$ dielectric insertion) to enable high-density, energy-efficient in-storage computation for hyperdimensional data processing.

**Key observables.** Search accuracy (>90% at QLC), Speedup ($\sim 1000	imes$), Energy Efficiency Improvement ($>10,000	imes$), Memory Window (MW) ($\sim 7.5$ V).

**Important parameters / regimes.** TB-scale datasets, QLC/TLC logic levels, $10^4$ P/E cycles, $14$ V programming voltage.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The planar device physics are assumed to be directly transferable to 3D vertical NAND architectures, and system performance relies on calibrated physics-based simulations.

**Figures summary.** Figures show SEM images of the FE-NAND strings, $I_D–V_G$ and MW–$V_{	ext{write}}$ characteristics demonstrating dielectric insertion and MW enhancement, and comparative performance plots against incumbent solutions.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem limitations, details the FE-NAND physical enhancement (dielectric insertion), demonstrates the core computation (MLC dot product), and finally benchmarks the system on large-scale search tasks, comparing it to other compute-in-memory approaches.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The growing demand for large-scale database search in data-intensive applications, ranging from proteomics to autonomous systems, has exposed fundamental limitations in von Neumann architectures due to memory bandwidth and energy constraints. Hyperdimensional (HD) computing offers a robust and parallelizable framework for such tasks, but its practical implementation remains challenged by high memory demands. Ultra-high-density, energy-efficient ferroelectric NAND (FE-NAND) memory provides a potential solution by enabling in-situ computation. We fabricate quad-level FE-NAND strings with wide memory windows, disturb resilience, and robust retention. Using these planar FE-NAND strings as building blocks, we experimentally demonstrate in-situ multi-level cell (MLC) dot product operations at the single-cell level and, using experimentally calibrated physics-based simulations, demonstrate Hamming similarity calculations between reference and query hypervectors (HV). This platform leverages the inherent error tolerance of HD computing to achieve >90% search accuracy even at high logic levels (TLC, QLC). When benchmarked on Open Modification Search (OMS) tasks in proteomics with TB-scale datasets, our system shows nearly 1,000x speedup and over 10,000x energy efficiency improvement compared to incumbent solutions. These results establish FE-NAND as a viable in-storage compute architecture for large-scale, high-dimensional data processing.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a comprehensive theoretical framework to predict the structural and functional properties of few-monolayer stacks in materials like SnSe. By combining DFT with combinatorial methods and statistical mechanics, the authors map the energy landscape, showing how stacking sequences determine key properties like ferroelectricity and nonlinear optical responses. This provides a powerful predictive tool for designing novel layered quantum materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous application of statistical mechanics (Boltzmann statistics) to predict the most probable structural phases in complex, interacting 2D systems is highly relevant for understanding phase transitions in quantum materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a general theoretical framework to classify and predict the stacking and physical properties (ferroelectric and nonlinear-optical) of few-monolayer stacks of identical (homo-) monolayers.

**Main result.** The study identifies that the stacking configurations are governed by a small number of point groups, and the energy landscape analysis predicts structural stability and transition barriers that suggest 'locking-in' at room temperature.

**Method.** The authors use Density Functional Theory (DFT) combined with a 'divide and conquer' combinatorial approach and Boltzmann statistics to map the energy landscape of stacking arrangements.

**Model / system.** The physical system is layered materials, specifically focusing on few-monolayer stacks of monochalcogenide (MC) compounds like SnSe. The model treats the stacking energy as a sum of pairwise interactions, allowing for the prediction of total energy for arbitrary stack numbers.

**Key observables.** Structural stability, symmetry (Layer Group and Point Group), interlayer stacking energy, in-plane electric dipole moment, and Second-Harmonic Generation (SHG) signals.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Energy barriers (e.g., > 40 meV/u.c.), temperature (finite-temperature effects), and the number of monolayers (N).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on DFT calculations for ground and metastable states, and the 'divide and conquer' model assumes identical lattice parameters between stacked layers.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the four stable bilayer structures, energy landscapes showing transition barriers, and plots detailing the probability of different stacking configurations as a function of temperature.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the DFT methods to find stable bilayers, then generalizing this to develop a combinatorial 'divide and conquer' approach for N-layers, and finally analyzing the resulting symmetry and temperature-dependent physical properties like ferroelectricity and SHG.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Structure leads to function: Knowing all possible ways to stack and slide identical monolayers enables the design of functionalities such as nonlinear optical responses and ferroelectricity in layered materials. Besides, mounting experimental evidence points to differing stacking configurations in few-monolayer and bulk samples. To exemplify the core concepts for stacking arbitrary monolayers, ground-state and metastable non-moiré SnSe stacks were first identified using density functional theory and employed to validate a ``divide and conquer'' combinatoral approach for determining the most probable stacking configurations in materials with an arbitrary number of identical monolayers. A small number of point groups accounts for all possible stacks, which explains experimental second-harmonic optical responses. Finite-temperature effects are also studied despite the granularity of available data. This comprehensive framework readily generalizes to provide a predictive description of arbitrary metastable few-homomonolayer stacks.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically examines the strain tunability of electron and hole g-factors in lead-halide perovskites. Using an advanced k.p model parameterized by DFT, the authors show that bulk g-factors can be significantly tuned by strain. Crucially, they contrast this with nanocrystals, where quantum confinement dampens the strain response.

**Why it may be interesting.** The strong theoretical link between structural strain, band structure modification, and spin properties (g-factors) is highly relevant for designing optoelectronic devices where external mechanical control is possible.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to theoretically investigate how external strain tunes the electron and hole g-factors in inorganic lead-halide perovskites, comparing bulk and nanocrystal behavior.

**Main result.** The bulk g-factors are highly tunable by external strain, potentially allowing tuning through zero, whereas the g-factors in nanocrystals are much less sensitive to strain due to quantum confinement effects.

**Method.** The research employs an 18-band k.p model, parameterized using DFT calculations (HSE06 functional), and calculates the g-factors using linear response theory.

**Model / system.** The physical system is $	ext{CsPb}X_3$ perovskites. The theoretical framework involves an 18-band k.p Hamiltonian, which is augmented by a strain term ($H(	ext{str})$) to model external strain effects.

**Key observables.** Electron and hole g-factors, and their dependence on external strain (hydrostatic, biaxial, uniaxial).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The k.p model uses 6 lowest-energy conduction bands and 12 highest-energy valence bands; the analysis considers various halide compositions ($	ext{Cl}, 	ext{Br}, 	ext{I}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The k.p model is an approximation, and the DFT calculations are performed for zero-temperature systems, neglecting phonon effects.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 shows the band structure for $	ext{CsPbBr}_3$ at the $\Gamma$ point, illustrating the irreducible representation of the relevant bands.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using the k.p model and DFT inputs, then calculates the strain dependence of the g-factors for the bulk material, and finally contrasts this with the reduced strain sensitivity observed in nanocrystals.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this paper, we theoretically study the electron and hole $g$-factors in inorganic lead-halide perovskites for the reference cubic phase. We employ an 18-band $k \cdot p$ model and determine its parameters using target band structures obtained from DFT calculations. We use the linear response theory to calculate the $g$-factors and investigate their dependence on external strain. We then perform real-space calculations of the electron and hole $g$-factors in perovskite nanocrystals. We show that the bulk $g$-factors can be tuned over a wide range by external strain. In some cases, strain can be used to tune the $g$-factor through zero. By contrast, the carrier $g$-factors in CsPb$X_3$ nanocrystals are considerably less sensitive to strain due to quantum confinement.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops Whitham modulation theory for the Davey-Stewartson (DS) system, a model for nonlinear wave packets coupled to a mean flow. By deriving and analyzing the resulting modulation equations, the authors determine the linear stability of the system's periodic traveling waves. The key finding is that only the defocusing DSII variant exhibits linear stability, providing crucial insight into the physical regimes where such wave trains can persist.

**Why it may be interesting.** The DS system is a fundamental model in nonlinear wave physics, relevant to optics and fluid dynamics. The application of modulation theory to determine stability in a mean-field coupled system provides general insights into the dynamics of 2D envelope equations.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops Whitham modulation theory for the Davey-Stewartson (DS) system and applies it to analyze the stability of its periodic traveling wave solutions.

**Main result.** The periodic solutions of the defocusing DSII system were found to be linearly stable, while all other variants of the DS system were determined to be unstable.

**Method.** The authors employed the multiple scales ansatz and derived the corresponding Whitham modulation equations by averaging the governing equations over the fast periodic variables.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on the Davey-Stewartson (DS) system, a canonical model describing weakly nonlinear wave packets in two spatial dimensions that interact resonantly with a slowly varying mean flow. The system has four variants determined by the signs of parameters $\sigma$ and $
u$.

**Key observables.** Linear stability of periodic solutions, the modulation equations themselves, and the dispersion relation $\omega = k_1v_1 - \sigma k_2v_2 - (k_2^2 - \sigma k_1^2)J / ho$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The parameters $\sigma$ and $
u$ define the four variants (DSII, DSI), and the small parameter $\epsilon$ governs the semiclassical scaling limit.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the validity of the modulation theory framework and that the wave parameters ($ho, \Phi, P, Q$) are periodic in the fast spatial variable $Z$.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by first establishing the governing equations for the DS system, then applying the multiple scales ansatz to derive the modulation equations, and finally using these equations to perform the stability analysis for the different system variants.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Davey-Stewartson (DS) system is a canonical model for a weakly nonlinear wave packet in two spatial dimensions that is resonantly coupled to the slowly varying mean flow it generates, and as such it governs modulated wave trains in settings as different as finite-depth water waves, quadratic optical media and magnetic films. Here we develop the Whitham modulation theory for the DS system and use it to study the stability of its periodic traveling wave solutions. Specifically: 1. We perform a detailed study of the parametric dependence of the periodic solutions of all four variants of the DS system, including their harmonic and soliton limits. 2. We present the formulation of Whitham modulation theory for the DS system and write down the resulting Whitham modulation equations for all four variants of the DS system. 3. We use the resulting modulation equations to study the stability of the periodic traveling wave solutions of all four variants of the DS system. 4. We validate the theoretical predictions by comparing them with a direct linearization of the DS system as well as with the direct numerical simulations of the DS system, showing excellent agreement. The results indicate that the periodic solutions of the defocusing DSII system are linearly stable, whereas those of all other variants of the DS system are unstable. The calculations also evidence many structural features (non-evolutionary modulation equations, constraints on the admissible initial data, and auxiliary mean-field constants absent from the traveling wave solutions yet indispensable to the modulation system) are expected to recur in any two-dimensional envelope equation with mean-field coupling.

</details>
